title: Project & setup
summary: Build, test, and understand the correctness-first CKKS GPU project.
text: ntt-gpu ¶ Exact GPU kernels for CKKS: NTT first, then base conversion, Hybrid key switching, and OpenFHE integration. The target workload is N=65,536 on RTX 5090, with RTX 4090 as the compatibility control. Current state: the CPU reference, Python oracle, portable GPU-schedule simulator, and OpenFHE transform/representation/Hybrid graph gates are implemented. CUDA source is ready; execution on a real GPU remains the next hardware gate. CPU simulation does not validate GPU barriers or launch behavior. Build & test ¶ Requires CMake, a C++20 compiler, and Python 3. CUDA is optional and detected automatically. cmake -S . -B build cmake --build build -j ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure The twelve portable checks cover vector generation at N=64/1024/65536, unit tests, the independent Python oracle, the shared device schedule, column and tile index/twiddle proofs in both directions, arithmetic exactness and full-size adversarial transforms, and the N=8 debug example. Small fixtures keep the quadratic oracle and schoolbook multiplication practical. With nvcc, three more gates compare CUDA with the same oracle and CPU reference. Array ordering, forward/inverse results, round trips, and polynomial multiplication must agree exactly. See run and debug to step through the N=8 example. Exact OpenFHE compatibility ¶ The optional gate pins OpenFHE 1.6.1 at b59e1f291965f14fbee5172cd83a20f5b856204f : bash scripts/openfhe_setup.sh It compares N=65536 NativePoly coefficient/evaluation conversions with our reference, including bit-reversed evaluation order. Its FirstPrime(50, ...) and LastPrime(59, ...) fixtures are 51- and 59-bit primes. Cases include zero, maximum, ramp, random coefficients, and independent random inverse inputs. A second gate, openfhe_representation_contract , checks exact evaluation indices, format-changing APIs, root selection, and three-tower DCRT packing at 50/55/60-bit primes. Read the D7 contract for the integration boundary and remaining scope. A third gate, openfhe_hybrid_graph , traces the exact Hybrid digit extension, key MAC, ModDown, and ciphertext wrapper graph at N=65536. It checks full and reduced levels with deterministic diagnostic keys and actual generated keys, using independent unreduced-CRT formulas. It requires the PKE library and the 64-bit, non-reduced-noise build; see the D8 graph . To reuse an installation, configure with -DNTT_ENABLE_OPENFHE_COMPAT=ON and set CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH to its install prefix. OpenFHE is not required for the standalone build. First session on a rented GPU ¶ bash scripts/autodl_setup.sh The script finds nvcc, updates source, builds, runs the gates, benchmarks N=65536, and writes hardware details and results to VERDICT.txt . Override the checkout, architecture, or benchmark arguments with NTT_REPO_DIR , NTT_CUDA_ARCH , and NTT_BENCH_ARGS . The default build targets sm_89 and, with CUDA 12.8+, sm_120 . For one known GPU, use -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native (CMake 3.24+). Design ¶ Both backends use the same negacyclic transform convention: psi is a primitive 2N-th root modulo q; psi^N = -1 forward: A_j = sum_i a_i * psi^((2j+1)*i) mod q input: natural coefficient order; output: bit-reversed evaluation order The CUDA schedule splits at 256. Pass 1 gathers 256 strided columns; pass 2 loads 256 contiguous rows. At N=65536, each pass handles eight stages in shared memory. One forward uses two launches and four logical array movements. The strided pass is uncoalesced, so logical bytes are not measured DRAM traffic. Stage bodies in dev_core.hpp are compiled for both CPU simulation and CUDA. The current __uint128_t remainder arithmetic is a correctness baseline. Shoup/Barrett reduction, coalesced layouts, and register staging are planned optimizations, subject to exact checks and profiling. Use the work-distribution explorer to inspect blocks, threads, pairs, and twiddle exponents. Roadmap ¶ Deliverable State CPU reference, oracle, schedule simulation Complete CUDA kernels and automatic GPU test registration Implemented; hardware validation pending Named-device baseline and tuning Planned Base conversion and Hybrid key switching Planned OpenFHE integration with CPU fallback Planned The v0.1 target is 2027-01-31; v0.2 key-switch/automorphism work targets 2027-04-30. See the tracked integration plan for working-day gates and the benchmark plan for measurements. Performance claims require named hardware and matching timing boundaries. Docs ¶ Start with NTT and butterflies , then CPU to CUDA . The implementation survey and GPU comparison explain the design choices. python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r docs/requirements.txt .venv/bin/python scripts/build_docs.py --check python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory build/docs-site Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ . See writing and publishing for editing, journals, and GitHub Pages export. Provenance ¶ Independent clean-room implementation. No code, data, or artifacts from past or present employers. Development history is recorded in git. License ¶ TBD before accepting outside contributions.

title: NTT & butterflies
summary: Direct sums, recursive butterflies, handwritten derivations, and an interactive stage/twiddle calculator.
text: ntt-gpu · a beginner's field guide NTT and butterflies. An NTT turns one expensive polynomial multiplication into many small, repeated butterfly operations. no prerequisites examples use mod 5 and mod 17 interactive diagrams × w a b a + w·b a − w·b the only shape this whole page needs The idea in four steps Read this first. The chapters below explain why each step is valid. 1 · Start A polynomial is stored as a list of coefficients. 2 · Transform The NTT evaluates that list at special modular points. 3 · Reuse A butterfly computes one shared sum-and-difference pair. 4 · Repeat N/2 butterflies across log₂N stages finish the transform. Shortest path: data → NTT → sum to butterfly → butterfly → network → negacyclic . The other chapters are optional detail. Contents 01 Input: coefficients 02 Special points 03 What the NTT does 04 Cost & savings 05 Sum → butterflies 05+ Derivation and twiddle factors 06 One butterfly 07 Full N = 8 network 09 Negacyclic NTT 10 Code mapping 01 Start with coefficients The input is a list of N numbers . In this page, that list represents a polynomial: 3 slot 0 7 slot 1 1 slot 2 9 slot 3 4 slot 4 0 slot 5 5 slot 6 2 slot 7 For this project, N is 65,536. We need to multiply two such lists efficiently: multiply two lists of length N, get back a list of length N The NTT (Number Theoretic Transform) is how that multiplication gets done fast. (How the product stays length N — the fold rule — is chapter 9's story.) 02 Choose special modular points Modulo 17, start at 1 and keep multiplying by 2. After eight different values, the sequence returns to 1: The wheel — the eight powers of 2, mod 17 · start at 1, keep multiplying by 2 1 2 4 8 16 15 13 9 ω⁰ ω¹ ω² ω³ ω⁴ = −1 ω⁵ ω⁶ ω⁷ dashed diameters: opposite points sum to 17 = q — each is the other's negative (property iii, halfway = minus) Eight different numbers, then the ninth step lands back on 1. The powers of 2 form a closed loop of exactly 8 points — a wheel . Such a number is a root of unity ("unity" just means 1): \(ω^N = 1\) , and primitive if no earlier power comes home. Everything the NTT relies on is a property of this wheel: Nothing sacred about 2 — mod 17 offers four primitive 8th roots: 2, 8, 9, 15. Each walks the same eight points in a different order; 2 just gives the easiest multiplication table. Optional: why these points make the NTT fast i. Closed: multiply = move Powers never leave the wheel: \(ω^{a}\,ω^{b} = ω^{a+b}\) — multiplying just adds positions, a clock for multiplication (the logarithm trick). Why: one number generates all N plug-in points, one multiplication each. ii. Distinct: nothing is lost A primitive root visits N different points, so N plugged-in values pin the list down exactly — the coordinates are reversible. Why: the transform has an inverse. The one demand on the prime: N | q−1 ( ntt.hpp:61 ). iii. Halfway = minus \(ω^{N/2} = -1\) : opposite points are negatives (above: 1↔16, 2↔15, 4↔13, 8↔9 — each pair sums to 17). Why: the ± that makes output pairs — the butterfly's two wings (chapter 6). iv. Squaring = a half wheel Every second point closes after N/2 steps: a half-size wheel with root ω². Why: wheels nest — the transform builds itself from half-size copies, the source of every "repeat" in chapter 5. Why not just any N distinct numbers? Any N distinct points make chapter 3's trick correct . Only wheel points make it fast : the shared brackets of chapter 5 are this wheel's symmetries showing up as algebra. The speed of the NTT is wheel symmetry. 03 What the NTT does A list like \((2, 1)\) is a tiny machine: plug a number t in for x, get a value out. And plugged-in values multiply one by one: \[(A\cdot B)(t) = A(t)\times B(t)\] One multiplication, no crossing terms — and it holds for every t. Both roads below use \(t = 2\) (mod 5); change any coefficient and they still agree: Interactive · two roads, one answer (mod 5) A slot 0 − 2 + A slot 1 · x − 1 + B slot 0 − 3 + B slot 1 · x − 2 + ROAD 1 · EXPAND BY HAND ROAD 2 · PLUG IN t = 2 ✓ the two roads agree Road 1 costs four multiplies and still knows the product at only one point. Road 2 costs one multiply — and the equation below runs Road 2 at every wheel point at once. To pin the product down we need its values at N different points — chapter 2's wheel supplies them. the definition · the whole transform in one line \[A_j = a_0+a_1\omega^j+a_2\omega^{2j}+a_3\omega^{3j}+\cdots \pmod{q}\] Evaluating the list at all N wheel points is the NTT . Output j is the list plugged in at wheel point ωʲ — and because the points are distinct (wheel property ii), the transform inverts: evaluate → multiply pointwise → invert replaces a list multiplication with N plain multiplies. The rest of this page makes that round trip cheap. Why "NTT" and not "FFT"? The FFT does this with decimals — but decimals round, and rounding errors compound. The NTT does the same idea with whole numbers mod a prime : exact forever. Its wheels exist whenever N | q−1 — checked at ntt.hpp:61 . 04 Direct evaluation vs butterflies: work saved The equation demands N outputs, each a sum of N products — computed one by one, that's \(N \times N\) multiplications per transform: Interactive · feel the N² pain list length N = 65,536 2 8 … 2 18 Radix-2 uses \(N/2\) butterflies in each of \(\log_2 N\) stages. At N=65536, direct evaluation forms 4,294,967,296 products ; the network uses 524,288 butterflies . The ratio is 8192:1 in these different counting units. Interactive · direct N² vs butterflies (N/2)·log₂N — log–log plot direct — each output on its own (N² products) butterflies — shared brackets ((N/2)·log₂N units) hover the plot — at N = 65,536 the direct line stands 8,192× above the butterfly line This compares arithmetic counts, not measured speed. A cyclic butterfly uses one multiply, one add and one subtract; this repository's folded negacyclic device butterfly uses two multiplies. CPU twiddle advancement adds another multiply. Doubling N multiplies the direct count by 4, and the butterfly count by \(2(\log_2N+1)/\log_2N\). The butterfly curve is slightly curved on a log–log plot. 05 Turn the NTT sum into butterflies Start from the ordinary NTT definition. For output index k, direct evaluation forms one N-term sum: \[ A_k = \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} a_r\,\omega^{rk}, \qquad 0\leq k<N \] Split the exact sum into even and odd input indices. Write \(r = 2m\) for even indices and \(r = 2m+1\) for odd indices: \[ \begin{aligned} \textcolor{#14655A}{E_k} &= \sum_{m=0}^{N/2-1} a_{2m}\,(\omega^2)^{mk} \\ \textcolor{#C2410C}{O_k} &= \sum_{m=0}^{N/2-1} a_{2m+1}\,(\omega^2)^{mk} \\[0.5em] A_k &= \textcolor{#14655A}{E_k} + \omega^k\,\textcolor{#C2410C}{O_k} \end{aligned} \] Now look at the output halfway around the wheel. Since \(ω^{N/2} = -1\) , its odd half changes sign while its even half does not: \[ \begin{aligned} A_{k+N/2} &= \textcolor{#14655A}{E_k} - \omega^k\,\textcolor{#C2410C}{O_k} \\ t &= \omega^k O_k \\[0.5em] (A_k,\ A_{k+N/2}) &= (E_k+t,\ E_k-t) \end{aligned} \] That final pair is one butterfly. The two outputs reuse the same \(E[k]\) , the same \(O[k]\) , and—most importantly—the same multiplication \(t = ω^k\,O[k]\) . 1 · DIRECT Compute N independent sums, each with N terms. \(\text{cost: } O(N^2)\) 2 · SPLIT Separate every sum into its even-index and odd-index terms. \(A=E+\omega^k O\) 3 · SHARE Pair outputs k and k+N/2. They share everything except a sign. \(E+t,\ E-t\) 4 · RECURSE E and O are smaller NTTs using the root ω². Split them again. \(\log_2 N\text{ stages}\) Why the optimization keeps working \(ω^{2}\) is an N/2-th root of unity, so E and O have exactly the same shape as the original problem, only half as large. Repeating the split reaches two-value problems. Each level contains N/2 butterflies, and there are log₂N levels. What exactly happens in each stage? For this cyclic DIT explanation, first place input coefficients in bit-reversed order. Stage s starts at zero, uses group width M and distance d, and combines two completed half-transforms. Every pair reads the previous stage and writes two new values: \[ M=2^{s+1},\quad d=M/2,\quad U=gM+j,\quad V=U+d,\quad 0\le j<d, \qquad t=\omega_N^{jN/M}X^{(s)}_V. \] \[ X^{(s+1)}_U=X^{(s)}_U+t,\qquad X^{(s+1)}_V=X^{(s)}_U-t. \] Stage 0 combines pairs into 2-point transforms; stage 1 combines two 2-point results into a 4-point result; stage s combines two d-point results into one M-point result. A stage has N/M groups and d butterflies per group, giving N/2 disjoint pairs. A later stage must wait until its input stage finishes. The complete numerical example in the negacyclic section uses the repository's opposite, DIF stage order. The handwritten derivation below expands N=4, recurses into the second split, and derives the twiddle exponent for every stage. Try its four-point arithmetic here first: Interactive · both levels, real numbers — mod 17, ω = 4 (ω² = 16 ≡ −1) a₀ − 3 + a₁ · x − 1 + a₂ · x² − 5 + a₃ · x³ − 2 + Change any coefficient: level 1 feeds level 2, four butterflies total — and the result is checked against the direct definition. One multiply, one add, one subtract; two values in, two out. That is the fast algorithm's only moving part. At N = 8 it simply nests one level deeper — chapter 7's machine, where we go next. 05+ Recursive decomposition and twiddle factors This derivation follows the handwritten notes from the even/odd split through a second recursion, a four-point network, and the twiddle exponent at every stage. It then connects those results to this repository's negacyclic DIF implementation. Notation In the ordinary NTT portion of the notes, φ denotes a primitive N-th root of unity ; here we write ω N , with ω N N/2 = −1. This repository uses ψ, a primitive 2N-th root of unity , with ψ N = −1 and ω N = ψ². The ordinary NTT requires N to divide q−1 and works modulo x N −1; the negacyclic form requires 2N to divide q−1 and works modulo x N +1. All arithmetic below is modulo a prime q, and N is a power of two. 1. Split one N-point NTT into two half-length NTTs Start with the definition: i indexes the input coefficients and j indexes the outputs. Split i into 2r and 2r+1: \[ \begin{aligned} b_j&=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}a_i\omega_N^{ij}\\ &=\sum_{r=0}^{N/2-1}a_{2r}\omega_N^{2rj} +\sum_{r=0}^{N/2-1}a_{2r+1}\omega_N^{(2r+1)j}\\ &=\underbrace{\sum_{r=0}^{N/2-1}a_{2r}(\omega_N^2)^{rj}}_{A_j} +\omega_N^j\underbrace{\sum_{r=0}^{N/2-1}a_{2r+1}(\omega_N^2)^{rj}}_{B_j}. \end{aligned} \] A is the N/2-point NTT of the even-index coefficients; B is the N/2-point NTT of the odd-index coefficients. Both use the root ω N ² = ω N/2 . Both are periodic in j with period N/2, so only 0 ≤ j < N/2。 \[ \begin{aligned} A_{j+N/2}&=A_j,\qquad B_{j+N/2}=B_j,\\ \omega_N^{j+N/2}&=-\omega_N^j,\\ b_j&=A_j+\omega_N^jB_j,\\ b_{j+N/2}&=A_j-\omega_N^jB_j. \end{aligned} \] This produces one butterfly pair: compute t = ω N j B j once, then output A j +t and A j −t . The output indices differ by N/2 and share one multiplication. 2. Recurse: where do ω² and ω⁴ come from? Split A's input sequence again. Its even and odd positions correspond to a 4r and a 4r+2 in the original array: \[ \begin{aligned} A_j&=\sum_{r=0}^{N/4-1}a_{4r}\omega_N^{4rj} +\omega_N^{2j}\sum_{r=0}^{N/4-1}a_{4r+2}\omega_N^{4rj}\\ &=C_j+\omega_N^{2j}D_j,\\ C_j&=\sum_{r=0}^{N/4-1}a_{4r}(\omega_N^4)^{rj},\qquad D_j=\sum_{r=0}^{N/4-1}a_{4r+2}(\omega_N^4)^{rj},\\ A_{j+N/4}&=C_j-\omega_N^{2j}D_j,\qquad 0\le j<N/4. \end{aligned} \] The minus sign follows from (ω N ²) N/4 = −1. Likewise, B splits into a 4r+1 and a 4r+3 . Each recursion halves the length and squares the root: ω N → ω N ² → ω N ⁴ → … , down to length 2. Bottom-up combination visits these lengths in the opposite order. 3. N=4: expand the sums and draw the network Let ω = ω 4 , so ω²=−1 and ω³=−ω. Expand all four outputs and regroup the shared intermediate values: \[ \begin{aligned} b_0&=a_0+a_1+a_2+a_3=(a_0+a_2)+(a_1+a_3),\\ b_1&=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3=(a_0-a_2)+\omega(a_1-a_3),\\ b_2&=a_0+a_1\omega^2+a_2\omega^4+a_3\omega^6=(a_0+a_2)-(a_1+a_3),\\ b_3&=a_0+a_1\omega^3+a_2\omega^6+a_3\omega^9=(a_0-a_2)-\omega(a_1-a_3). \end{aligned} \] The first level computes P=a₀+a₂, Q=a₀−a₂, R=a₁+a₃ and S=a₁−a₃. The second combines P and R into b₀ and b₂, and Q and S into b₁ and b₃. Only the latter pair needs a multiplication by ω. Four-point NTT: two levels and four butterflies Inputs a0 and a2 produce P and Q; a1 and a3 produce R and S. P and R produce b0 and b2; Q and omega times S produce b1 and b3. Outputs are drawn in the order b0, b2, b1, b3. a₀ a₁ a₂ a₃ P = a₀+a₂ R = a₁+a₃ Q = a₀−a₂ S = a₁−a₃ b₀ = P+R b₂ = P−R b₁ = Q+ωS b₃ = Q−ωS Level 1: factor 1 Level 2: factor 1 or ω + − + − × ω Each pair shares its intermediate values; four butterflies complete the transform. Scroll horizontally on small screens. The drawing groups outputs as b₀, b₂, b₁, b₃ to show shared intermediates; the mathematical output index is still j. The drawing's vertical order does not prescribe memory order. Standard iterative DIT usually starts with bit-reversed inputs and produces natural-order outputs. This repository's forward DIF takes natural-order inputs and produces bit-reversed evaluations. See the N=8 network and the D7 representation contract for the exact ordering. 4. Derive the stage twiddle from its length Use the notes' bottom-up DIT combination , with s starting at zero. Stage s combines two 2 s -point results into one M=2 s+1 -point result. Here j is the offset within the current butterfly group. \[ \begin{aligned} M&=2^{s+1},\qquad 0\le s<\log_2N,\qquad 0\le j<M/2,\\ \omega_M&=\omega_N^{N/M},\\ w_{s,j}&=\omega_M^j=\left(\omega_N^{N/2^{s+1}}\right)^j =\boxed{\omega_N^{jN/2^{s+1}}}. \end{aligned} \] A butterfly's factor follows from three quantities: stage s → group length M → local offset j . Groups in the same stage share the j-to-factor rule. The group number changes the array positions, not the exponent. Read the sequence 8; 4,12; 2,10,6,14 For N=16 and four-bit reversal, these entries are rev₄(1)…rev₄(15). For example, reversing 0001 gives 1000=8; reversing 0011 gives 1100=12. Table index k rev₄(k) 1 8 2, 3 4, 12 4…7 2, 10, 6, 14 8…15 1, 9, 5, 13, 3, 11, 7, 15 If a root table is defined as T[k]=r rev₄(k) , the table above lists its exponents. These numbers alone do not define the order of r, the transform direction, or the butterfly schedule. They are not a universal cyclic DIT twiddle list . In particular, this repository's natural power table and OpenFHE's bit-reversed root table are distinct. See D7's root and cache contract 。 6. Connect the derivation to the forward negacyclic loop The repository's forward transform is DIF. Stage t starts at zero, and distance d=N/2 t+1 decreases. For group length M=2d and local offset J: \[ \begin{aligned} E&=\frac{N}{2d}J,\qquad w=\omega_N^E=\psi^{(N/d)J},\qquad c=\psi^d,\\ (u,v)&\longmapsto\bigl(u+cv,\;(u-cv)w\bigr)\pmod q. \end{aligned} \] The change-of-root rule still raises the global root to N/M, but stages run in the opposite direction and include c to fold the negacyclic twist. At N=65536 the first forward stage has d=32768 and w=ω N J =ψ 2J . In the final stage d=1, J must be 0 and w=1. DIT stage 0 is not the first stage of the repository's forward DIF. The inverse uses reciprocal w and c, reverses the stage order, and finally multiplies by N⁻¹. For the exact coefficient indices, bit-reversed output order, and CUDA groups, see the forward and inverse work distribution 。 06 Meet the butterfly A butterfly takes two inputs and produces a sum and a weighted difference. The crossing wires give the circuit its name. These two common forms place the multiplier on different legs: × w + − a b a + b·w a − b·w 1 2 DIT — ① multiply the input , ② add / subtract · what chapters 5–7 derive + − × w a b a + b (a − b)·w 1 2 DIF — ① add / subtract, ② multiply the difference output · the same unit, run the other way Same two wings — only the order of multiply vs ± differs (the gold ①②). DIT multiplies before the crossing, DIF after it. (The repo's negacyclic forward adds one refinement on top of DIF — a ladder constant ψ^d on the input leg; that is chapter 10's loop.) 07 Connect butterflies into stages Eight wires, values flowing left to right; every X is one butterfly. Press play (arithmetic mod 17, ω = 2), or click any butterfly to inspect it. The partner distance doubles each stage — 1, 2, 4 — the recursion of chapter 5, unrolled one level more and laid out flat. Interactive · the N = 8 butterfly network (mod 17) ▶ play all stages next stage ⏭ reset stage 0 / 3 — values not yet transformed Hover or click a butterfly (the X crossings) to see exactly what it computes. wire (a value flowing right) butterfly value chip (appears as stages complete) Why are the inputs scrambled? The leftmost values are in bit-reversed order (0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7 — index in binary, read backwards). That one upfront shuffle lets every stage read its partners from nearby positions and the outputs arrive in natural order. The repo ships the mirror image: a DIF forward (natural inputs, bit-reversed outputs ) paired with a DIT inverse that consumes exactly that order — so in the real pipeline the two permutations cancel and no bit-reversal pass exists at all ( bitrev.hpp documents the permutation itself). And the negacyclic variant? This network is the plain ("cyclic") transform. The negacyclic variant below uses the same pair network with a folded ψ factor on the lower input of each butterfly ( ntt.hpp:87 ). 09 CKKS uses the negacyclic form One loose end from chapter 1: the operation there was "multiply two lists, get back a list of the same length N ." But plain multiplication lengthens the list: \[(2+x)(3+2x)=6+7x+2x^2\] If every multiplication grew the list, nothing could chain. The fix is one fold rule, in exactly two flavors: \[ \begin{aligned} x^N &= +1 && \text{cyclic: wrap with a plus} \\ x^N &= -1 && \text{negacyclic: wrap with a minus} \end{aligned} \] The cyclic fold is precisely the world of chapters 3–7: every ω-wheel point satisfies x^N = ω^N = 1. The negacyclic fold is the one this repo implements. With \(x^{2} = -1\) (N = 2, mod 5), the overflow folds back like this: \[ 6+7x+2x^2 \;\longmapsto\; (6-2)+7x \;\equiv\; 4+2x \pmod{5} \] All numbers live mod some prime (here mod 5) — only the remainder after dividing survives, so numbers stay tiny forever. Which points respect the minus fold? Those with \(x^N = -1\) — the roots of \(x^N + 1\) . They are the odd steps of a doubled wheel: a number ψ with \(ψ^N = -1\) closes after 2N points, and \((ψ^{\mathrm{odd}})^N = (-1)^{\mathrm{odd}} = -1\) . Mod 17, ψ = 6, and \(ψ^{2} = ω\) — its even steps are chapter 2's wheel: The doubled wheel · ψ = 6, a 16-th root of unity mod 17 (ψ⁸ = −1, ψ² = ω) even steps = the ω wheel: 1 ψ⁰ 2 ψ² 4 ψ⁴ 8 ψ⁶ 16 ψ⁸ 15 ψ¹⁰ 13 ψ¹² 9 ψ¹⁴ odd steps = negacyclic: 6 ψ¹ 12 ψ³ 7 ψ⁵ 14 ψ⁷ 11 ψ⁹ 5 ψ¹¹ 10 ψ¹³ 3 ψ¹⁵ spot-check one highlighted point: 6⁸ = (6²)⁴ = 2⁴ = 16 ≡ −1 (mod 17) ✓ · chapter 3's t = 2 mod 5 was exactly an odd step of the small doubled wheel there (2² ≡ −1, 2⁴ ≡ 1) The key substitution: pre-twist, then use the ordinary NTT Let \(ω = ψ^{2}\) and pre-twist coefficient r as \(b[r] = a[r]\,ψ^r\) . An ordinary cyclic NTT of b then gives \(\sum_{r=0}^{N-1} b_r\omega^{rk} = \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} a_r\psi^{(2k+1)r}\) . In other words, the twist moves evaluation from the even powers of ψ to exactly the odd powers—the roots of x^N+1. The inverse runs the cyclic inverse and multiplies coefficient r by \(ψ^{-r}\) . Derive the factors from the first split Choose a primitive 2N-th root ψ in the current prime field, so ψᴺ=−1, and set ω=ψ². For power-of-two N, checking ψᴺ=−1 proves that ψ has order 2N. The prime must satisfy \(2N\mid(q-1)\). OpenFHE compatibility additionally requires the exact same ψ as its tower parameters; another primitive root changes the output order. \[ F_k=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}a_i\psi^{(2k+1)i} =\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}(a_i\psi^i)\omega^{ki}. \] Now split input into a low half and a high half, d=N/2. This is the DIF split; the even/odd split above was DIT. The high-half factor contains a sign that depends only on k: \[ \begin{aligned} F_k&=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\left[a_j+a_{j+d}\psi^{(2k+1)d}\right]\psi^{(2k+1)j},\\ \psi^{(2k+1)d}&=\psi^d(\psi^N)^k=(-1)^k\psi^d. \end{aligned} \] Separate the even output indices k=2ℓ and odd indices k=2ℓ+1. Both smaller transforms use root ψ², but the odd branch needs an extra ψ²ʲ: \[ \begin{aligned} F_{2\ell}&=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\underbrace{(a_j+\psi^d a_{j+d})}_{x_j}(\psi^2)^{(2\ell+1)j},\\ F_{2\ell+1}&=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\underbrace{(a_j-\psi^d a_{j+d})\psi^{2j}}_{y_j}(\psi^2)^{(2\ell+1)j}. \end{aligned} \] The first split gives c=ψᴺᐟ² and w=ψ²ʲ. To derive all later folded factors without guessing a root for each branch, compare with the ordinary cyclic DIF network applied to the pre-twisted coefficients. At a current block of length 2d, let its cyclic values and folded values be related by \(b_j=\psi^j a_j\), where j is local to that block. The cyclic butterfly reads \(b_{j+d}=\psi^{j+d}a_{j+d}\): \[ \begin{aligned} b'_j&=b_j+b_{j+d}=\psi^j(a_j+\psi^d a_{j+d}),\\ b'_{j+d}&=(b_j-b_{j+d})\omega_N^{jN/(2d)} =\psi^j(a_j-\psi^d a_{j+d})\omega_N^{jN/(2d)}. \end{aligned} \] Both child blocks now have length d and local index j. Removing their common local twist ψʲ leaves the folded outputs \(x_j=a_j+\psi^d a_{j+d}\) and \(y_j=(a_j-\psi^d a_{j+d})\omega_N^{jN/(2d)}\). The same relation holds for the next split with d halved. Initially it is exactly the pre-twist; at length one j=0, so the remaining twist is 1. This proves every stage and the final result with no extra twist pass. What stays the same The radix-2 network, paired indices, number of stages, and N/2 butterflies per stage do not change. \[ \begin{aligned} u' &= u+v \\ v' &= (u-v)\,w \end{aligned} \] What negacyclic changes The ψ twist changes the factors carried by the butterfly. This repo folds it into the same pass instead of storing a separate twist table. \[ \begin{aligned} u' &= u+cv \\ v' &= (u-cv)\,w \end{aligned} \] For the repo's forward DIF loop, a stage pairs entries distance \(d\) apart. Its folded factors are: \[ \begin{aligned} c_d &= \psi^d \\ w_{d,j} &= \psi^{\frac{N}{d}j} = \omega^{\frac{N}{2d}j} \\[0.5em] \mathrm{upper}' &= \mathrm{upper}+c_d\,\mathrm{lower} \\ \mathrm{lower}' &= (\mathrm{upper}-c_d\,\mathrm{lower})\,w_{d,j} \end{aligned} \] The group number does not select the twiddle . At a fixed stage, every group repeats the same sequence: j starts at 0, so \(w = 1\) , then advances by \(ψ^{N/d}\) for each butterfly offset. Negacyclic therefore changes the factors, not the network's pairing pattern. The inverse uses reciprocal ψ factors, reverses the stage direction, and applies the final \(N^{-1}\) scale. 10 Map the picture to code Here is the actual loop from this repo's CPU reference ( include/ntt/ntt.hpp , the forward DIF sweep — twist folded in as ladder constants, natural values in, bit-reversed values out). Read the comments with chapter 7 open next to it — every line is a part of the picture: for ( uint64_t stage_pair_distance = n_ / 2 ; stage_pair_distance >= 1 ; stage_pair_distance >>= 1 ) { const uint64_t ladder_twiddle = pow_mod (psi_, stage_pair_distance, q_); // c_d = ψ^d const uint64_t twiddle_step = pow_mod (psi_, n_ / stage_pair_distance, q_); // ψ^(N/d) for ( uint64_t group_start_index = 0 ; group_start_index < n_; group_start_index += 2 * stage_pair_distance) { uint64_t twiddle_power = 1 ; // j = 0 for ( uint64_t pair_offset = 0 ; pair_offset < stage_pair_distance; ++pair_offset) { const uint64_t upper_index = group_start_index + pair_offset; const uint64_t lower_index = upper_index + stage_pair_distance; const uint64_t upper_value = values[upper_index]; const uint64_t scaled_lower_value = mul_mod (ladder_twiddle, values[lower_index], q_); values[upper_index] = add_mod (upper_value, scaled_lower_value, q_); // upper + c_d·lower values[lower_index] = mul_mod ( sub_mod (upper_value, scaled_lower_value, q_), twiddle_power, q_); // (upper − c_d·lower)·w_d,j twiddle_power = mul_mod (twiddle_power, twiddle_step, q_); } } } Three nested loops, one idea: for every butterfly in every stage — u+v, u−v. The CUDA port assigns independent pairs to threads and fuses several stages inside a shared-memory block. At N=65536, one forward transform uses two launches; it does not launch a separate kernel for every stage. Recap The NTT evaluates a polynomial at modular roots of unity. Reusing even/odd subtransforms reduces N² direct products to (N/2)·log₂N butterflies. At N=65,536 that is 524,288 butterflies. CKKS uses odd powers of a primitive 2N-th root, giving multiplication modulo x^N+1. ntt-gpu · docs/butterfly-explained.html mod-5 & mod-17 examples · local KaTeX · view source freely Nov 2026

title: From CPU to CUDA
summary: Threads, blocks, shared memory, and this repository's two-pass GPU schedule.
text: ntt-gpu · a beginner's field guide to the GPU port From CPU to CUDA. Each GPU thread handles a butterfly pair. Blocks keep small tiles in shared memory so several stages run without repeated VRAM traffic. target: RTX 5090 ring dimension: 65,536 256 threads per block every cook, same step, own ingredient The GPU plan in four steps This is the whole design. The chapters below explain the hardware and show the current code. 1 · SPLIT Give each independent butterfly pair to a GPU thread. 2 · LOAD A block gathers one 256-value group into shared memory. 3 · COMPUTE Run several stages locally, with a barrier between stages. 4 · REGROUP Use a far-pair pass and a near-pair pass to cover the full NTT. Current status: correctness-first baseline. Results must match the OpenFHE-compatible CPU reference exactly. The strided pass is not yet coalesced, so “four logical movements” does not mean four efficient VRAM transactions. Contents 01 CPU vs GPU 02 GPU vocabulary 03 Parallel butterflies 04 Two-pass design 05 Shared-memory tile 06 Code mapping 07 Synchronization 08 Memory cost 09 Current limits 01 CPU and GPU favor different work A CPU is good at a few complicated tasks. A GPU is good at many copies of the same small task. A GPU schedules groups of 32 threads called warps . Threads in a warp normally execute the same instruction on different data; different warps can make progress independently. Branch divergence can reduce efficiency within a warp. At each NTT stage, disjoint pairs use the same butterfly formula. Assigning these pairs to threads exposes parallel work without changing the result. 02 Six GPU terms These six terms connect the GPU model to this repository. Word Plain meaning In this repo thread One execution instance. It computes assigned pairs; it does not permanently own a coefficient. we use T = 256 per block block A team of threads sharing memory and block barriers. one block owns one tile grid All blocks in a launch. The x and y coordinates identify independent work. x = tile index, y = RNS limb shared memory Fast storage shared by the threads of one block. 256 values = 2 KB per limb global memory Device-wide memory holding coefficients, moduli, and twiddle tables. the whole polynomial, all limbs kernel A function launched across a grid of threads. six kernels in ntt_kernels.cu A barrier ( __syncthreads() in code) is the station's roll call: every cook in the block must arrive before anyone leaves. Chapter 7 is about the one way to misuse it. how the pieces nest · one picture HOST your Mac / the CLI starts the kernel launch GPU — one chip GLOBAL MEMORY (VRAM) — the warehouse · shared by every block BLOCK (x=0, y=1) its counter (shared) BLOCK (x=1, y=1) its counter (shared) BLOCK (x=2, y=1) its counter (shared) every block loads its tile from VRAM, computes on its counter, writes back — blocks never see each other's counters thread (a cook) → inside a block (a station, with its private counter) → blocks tile the grid (x = tile, y = limb) → all inside one GPU around one warehouse Optional: RTX 4090 and RTX 5090 capacity estimates the picture, counted · for both rentable cards RTX 4090 RTX 5090 station groups (SMs) 128 170 cooks in flight (resident threads) 196,608 261,120 our 256-cook stations, resident at once 768 1,020 max cooks per block / per station 1,024 / 1,536 1,024 / 1,536 counter (shared) per block · per station 48 KB · ~100 KB 48 KB · ~100 KB warehouse (VRAM) 24 GB GDDR6X 32 GB GDDR7 pipe into the chip — VRAM bandwidth ≈ 1.0 TB/s ≈ 1.8 TB/s traffic inside the chip — shared, aggregate ≈ 40 TB/s ≈ 50 TB/s The design fact hiding in the last two rows: on-chip traffic is 40–50× the pipe into the chip — the entire reason the communication ladder (chapter 5) exists. Aggregate shared figures are order-of-magnitude estimates (per-SM path × SMs × boost clock); the ratio is the point, not the decimals. // the first rows are one multiplication chain — the table explains itself: 4090: 128 SMs × 1,536 threads/SM = 196,608 in flight ÷ 256 (our T) = 768 of our blocks resident 5090: 170 SMs × 1,536 = 261,120 ÷ 256 = 1,020 These are thread-limit ceilings, not measured occupancy. Registers, shared memory, and block limits can reduce residency. At 40 limbs each pass launches 10,240 blocks; the scheduler runs them as resources become available. At N = 65,536 with 3 limbs, each pass launches 256 × 3 = 768 blocks . How many stay resident at once depends on threads, registers, shared memory, and the device's block limits; measure it instead of assuming one wave. 03 One stage has independent pairs Recall the NTT's shape: at every stage, the list is chopped into pairs, and each pair goes through one butterfly. At N = 16, one stage has eight disjoint pairs. Follow both the indices and the values: Follow all four stages at N=16 below. Every stage has eight independent pairs; stage boundaries carry dependencies. The two worked groups show how the first two stages stay inside strided columns and the last two stay inside contiguous rows. Earlier 8-point pairing animation one stage at N = 8 · click a stage stage d = 4 stage d = 2 stage d = 1 pick 0,2,4,6 → 2 stages Every element belongs to exactly one pair per stage — the four butterflies share nothing . Four cooks, zero talking, any order. The fourth button is pass 1 of the real port in miniature (chapter 4). That "share nothing" is the entire secret. Because the pairs are disjoint , the four butterflies of a stage can run simultaneously, interleaved, in any order, on any cook — the final list is identical every time . A GPU stage is just: hand each pair to a cook, let them all fly at once, wait for the slowest, next stage. Disjointness also buys locality : a stage with distance d only ever pairs values inside one 2d-wide group, so a group of 2 k values owns its k smallest stages outright — the fact chapter 4 turns into the two-pass split, taken once with strided groups and once with contiguous tiles. Hold onto that sentence — it is also why a plain CPU simulator, running the same stage bodies serially, can prove the whole schedule before any GPU is rented. 04 Split the NTT into two passes So why not one giant block that does the whole transform? Size — a block's counter is capped at 48 KB, and the data is far bigger: where "1.5 MB" comes from · why the data can't sit on one counter 1 value (one coefficient, one limb) = 64 bits = 8 bytes one limb = 2¹⁶ values × 8 bytes = 524,288 B = 512 KB this repo = 3 limbs × 512 KB = 1,536 KB ≈ 1.5 MB real FHE = ~40 limbs × 512 KB ≈ 20 MB = 427× a block's whole 48 KB counter More limbs ≠ harder: each limb is one independent column of the grid (the y address) doing the identical dance — real coefficients are thousands of bits, kept as ~40 machine-word residues, one transform each. So how should a GPU run this? Walk the same road the port had to walk — four steps, each one forced by the step before: ① How the CPU does it — and where it hurts The reference ( ntt.hpp ) is one cook walking the list in order: stage by stage, pair by pair. At N = 8 that's four butterflies, one after another — even though chapter 3 proved they're independent. The picture below is the whole problem in miniature: same four butterflies, four units of wall time versus one . Fine at lecture size — but a real forward is 32,768 × 16 ≈ 524,288 butterflies per limb , ~21 million across 40 limbs. One cook at a few GHz drowns; that's the wall. ② First GPU idea: every pair on a cook, everything from VRAM Hand each pair of each stage to its own cook, all cooks at once, everyone reading and writing the warehouse directly. This works — and it is what a naive port does for every stage. But now count truck trips: every stage fetches its partners from VRAM and writes them back — one round-trip per stage per value, and there are 16 stages. The cooks spend their day at the loading dock (chapter 8's ladder: warehouse ≈ ×400 the counter). Both modular arithmetic and memory traffic require profiling. ③ The hardware rule that shapes the fix — and the one choice we get to make The fast counter is private to a block — 256 cooks sharing 48 KB — and nobody outside the block can touch it. So a stage can escape the warehouse on one condition: all its pairs must sit inside data one block can gather onto its counter . The group size is ours to choose; the port picks 256 : counter budget: 48 KB ÷ 8 bytes per value = up to 6,144 values per group choose: 256 values (= 2 KB of the 48) — and 65,536 = 256 × 256 Why 256 exactly? It must be a power of two , so groups always contain whole pair-groups with nothing straddling an edge. And at N = 65,536 it makes the bookkeeping symmetric: 256 groups of 256 values , twice over — once strided, once contiguous (rung ④). Each block requests 2 KiB of shared memory; actual residency also depends on registers and hardware limits. one block's counter budget: 48 KB 2 KB spare — 46 KB of the allowance unused one SM station — neighbors bring their own tiles: 2 KB group block A 2 KB group block B 2 KB group block C ④ That number is the pair distance d Look at a pair's addresses when the list is viewed as a 256×256 grid (row = 256q + r): partners of a far stage (d a multiple of 256) have the same r — same column, different row — so each strided group {r, r+256, r+512, …} owns all far stages. Partners of a near stage (d ≤ 128) sit in the same row — a contiguous 256-tile owns all near stages. Two groupings, no third case. Stated cleanly, the four steps compress into one rule — the one structural idea of this port: the two-pass split · groups of 256, twice PASS 1 — the strided groups (d = 32,768 … 256) → 256 groups {r, r+256, …} each gather to a counter, run 8 stages, scatter PASS 2 — the contiguous tiles (d = 128 … 1) → 256 tiles of 256 each gather, run 8 stages, scatter Both passes run the same butterflies as the CPU reference. Pass 1 handles far pairs; pass 2 handles near pairs. This is four logical value movements, but pass 1 currently uses strided, uncoalesced addresses, so the hardware may issue many more memory transactions. 05 Keep a group in shared memory Global memory is the warehouse; shared memory is the counter. A shared-phase block does exactly four things: one block, one group · the kernel's whole life VRAM (global) the polynomial BLOCK — 256 cooks x = group id · y = limb 0..2 the block's COUNTER — 2 KB 256 values · 1 fetch in + 1 write out, total 1 2 4 3 8 stages · d = 128…1 · barrier each ① 256 cooks gather 256 values (1 each) · ② roll call — values land on the counter · ③ eight butterfly stages, barrier between · ④ carry the results back Naive code reads and writes VRAM at every stage. The two-pass design loads and stores each group once per pass. That reduces logical traffic, but pass 1 still needs a coalesced transpose or Four-Step layout to make those accesses efficient. A 256-value group uses 2 KB of shared memory per limb, leaving room for several blocks to reside on an SM. Actual occupancy on the RTX 5090 must be measured after register use and launch limits are known. The same trick, taken twice Notice what the tile trick actually was: a group of 2^k values hosts the k smallest-distance stages with zero outside communication . The port takes this trick twice — once with strided groups, once with contiguous ones — and that is the whole two-pass split: one forward at N = 65,536 · two passes, four truck trips PASS 1 strided groups {r, r+256, …} × 256 groups × 3 limbs 8 stages d = 32,768…256 8 stages on its counter 8 stages on its counter VRAM — the warehouse · the mix: pass 1 scatters strided, pass 2 gathers contiguous 8 stages d = 128…1 8 stages on its counter 8 stages on its counter PASS 2 contiguous tiles 256q … 256q+255 × 256 tiles × 3 limbs 1 2 3 4 per value: ① fetch + ② write-back + ③ fetch + ④ write-back = 4 warehouse trips — versus 16 naive Two things this shape fixes at once. The order differs from stage order only in grouping — the forward runs pass 1 then pass 2, the inverse runs the same ladder backwards. And every launch is self-contained: two kernel launches per forward (one per pass), each block needing nothing but its own 256 values. 06 Map the design to code Everything above exists in the repo in three small pieces. First, the butterfly body itself — written once , in include/ntt/dev_core.hpp , with the loop arranged as "one cook's slice of the pairs": // one DIF stage, one thread's slice — the same body the CPU simulator runs NTT_DEV void dev_dif_stage (uint64_t* tile, uint64_t tile_len, uint64_t d, uint64_t n, const uint64_t* pp, uint64_t q, uint32_t tid, uint32_t nthr) { const uint64_t lg = log2_of_pow2(d); for (uint64_t p = tid; p < tile_len / 2 ; p += nthr) { // MY pairs: start at my // thread id, stride by the thread count — chapter 3's disjoint pairs const uint64_t g = p >> lg, j = p & (d - 1 ); // which group, which offset const uint64_t u = (g << (lg + 1 )) + j, v = u + d; // the pair's two slots const uint64_t x = tile[u]; const uint64_t cv = mul_mod(pp[d], tile[v], q); // ladder constant ψ^d tile[u] = add_mod(x, cv, q); tile[v] = mul_mod(sub_mod(x, cv, q), pp[(n >> lg) * j], q); // twiddle } } Second, the pass-1 kernel — pure choreography around the stage bodies, in src/cuda/ntt_kernels.cu . One block owns one strided group, start to finish: __global__ void dif_col_kernel (uint64_t* a, const uint64_t* pp, const uint64_t* q, uint64_t n, uint32_t sub) { extern __shared__ uint64_t smem[]; // the counter const uint64_t r = blockIdx.x; // x = which strided group uint64_t* al = a + ( uint64_t )blockIdx.y * n; // y = which limb for (uint32_t t = threadIdx.x; t < sub; t += blockDim.x) // ① gather: value r+256t, smem[t] = al[r + ( uint64_t (t) << 8 )]; // one per cook __syncthreads(); // ② roll call for (uint64_t delta = sub / 2 ; delta >= 1 ; delta >>= 1 ) { // ③ the 8 far stages, dev_dif_col_stage(smem, sub, delta, n, pp, q, threadIdx.x, blockDim.x, r); __syncthreads(); // barrier each } for (uint32_t t = threadIdx.x; t < sub; t += blockDim.x) // ④ scatter back strided al[r + ( uint64_t (t) << 8 )] = smem[t]; } The pass-2 kernel ( dif_tile_kernel ) is the same shape with a contiguous gather — it is this kernel with r + (t<<8) replaced by base + t , running the near stages with dev_dif_stage . Third, the launches — where the grid's two addresses become the map of the whole problem. Remember RNS from the butterfly guide: the same transform runs once per limb (per prime), completely independently, so the y address is the limb: // one forward = TWO launches (grid = x × limbs): dif_col_kernel<<< dim3 ( 256 , num_limbs), T, sub * sizeof (uint64_t)>>>(buf, d_pp, d_q, n, sub); dif_tile_kernel<<< dim3 (n/ 256 , num_limbs), T, 256 * sizeof (uint64_t)>>>(buf, d_pp, d_q, n, 256 ); // pass 1: block (x=r, y=k) = strided group r of limb k — owns {r, r+256, …} // pass 2: block (x=q, y=k) = contiguous tile q of limb k — owns 256q … 256q+255 Three limbs produce 768 blocks per pass. The y grid coordinate batches limbs in one launch; hardware resource limits determine how many blocks run at once. And the communication between stages — the part that makes or breaks a GPU program — is different in each phase, by design: ⇄ Between the two passes: the mix is pure data movement Pass 2's inputs are pass 1's outputs, regrouped — strided scatter becomes contiguous gather. No thread waits on another explicitly: the two launches share one stream, and pass 2 cannot begin until pass 1's writes have landed in VRAM. The pass boundary and the kernel boundary are the same line. ⇄ Between stages inside a pass: the barrier, because partners swap On the counter, the values your thread reads at stage d were written at stage 2d by different threads of your block — the crossing re-shuffles ownership every stage. That is the entire reason for __syncthreads() after each stage: all 256 cooks finish, then anyone may read. ∅ Between blocks: silence — and that is the design Inside either pass, every block's 256 values are a self-contained problem — a strided group for pass 1, a tile for pass 2 — and no pair ever leaves them. With three limbs, each pass has 768 independent block-local stage groups, which is why one launch finishes eight whole stages , and why the GPU can pack blocks onto SMs in any arrangement it likes. 07 Synchronize between stages Two GPU habits bite newcomers, and both are already handled in the kernel — know them when you read it. the roll call rule · why barriers sit between stages the barrier — nobody passes alone cook A — done early cook B — working cook C — nearly there cook D — the slowest waiting… still working all cross together — when D arrives time → a block is exactly as fast as its slowest thread — so keep everyone's work the same shape Rule 1: the barrier is all-or-nothing Every thread of a block must reach every __syncthreads() . Put one inside an if that only some threads take, and the others wait forever — a hung kernel. That is why our barriers sit between stage loops, never inside the pair loop: all 256 cooks finish their slice, then everyone crosses together. Rule 2: idle cooks still attend roll call At N = 64 the tile is 64 values — only 32 pairs — but the block still has 256 threads. Most cooks hold no pair. Their loop body simply does zero iterations ( for (p = tid; p < 32; p += 256) never starts), and they walk straight to the barrier. Harmless — as long as they don't skip it . The repo's n=64 test fixture exists precisely to keep this edge honest. 08 Memory movement sets the pace The whole design — tiles, phases, staging — is really one decision: which shelf does each number live on? The shelves differ by orders of magnitude: cost to fetch one value · relative, order-of-magnitude Log-scale bars — each gridline is ×10. Exact cycles vary by GPU generation; the gaps are what matter. In kitchen terms: registers are in your hands, shared is on your station's counter, global is the warehouse across town, and copying from the host computer is a delivery truck. Our kernel's shape follows directly: start and end in the warehouse, stage the tile on the counter, keep loop counters and twiddles in hands — and never, ever truck data back and forth per stage. This ladder is also why the multiply pipeline stays on the GPU end to end: two forwards, pointwise, one inverse, then one truck trip home. 09 Current baseline and next optimizations Everything above is proven before any rental: the stage bodies live once in dev_core.hpp , compiled by a CPU simulator that must match the reference exactly — the rented GPU's gates then check only the thin kernel wrappers. One confession before you read the benchmarks: version 1 of the GPU arithmetic is deliberately unoptimized. The multiply inside every butterfly uses the same __uint128_t division as the CPU reference — because on the GPU that division is emulated : the hardware has no 128-bit divide, so the compiler builds one from many instructions. Every butterfly pays it. That is the right order of operations: make it right, measure the gap, then make it fast . The bench table's job is to quantify exactly how slow v1 is — the CPU reference column is right there in the same table. The fix (Barrett or Montgomery reduction: division-free modular multiplication, the standard trick every production NTT uses) swaps in later behind the same function signature, with its own dedicated cross-check. The first RTX 5090 run answers one question: does N=65536 match the reference exactly across the target modulus widths? Then benchmarks should isolate modular reduction, coalescing, radix, register pressure, and end-to-end transfer cost. Recap Each thread computes butterfly pairs. Each block loads one group into shared memory, runs several stages with barriers, and writes the group back. A far-pair pass followed by a near-pair pass covers the full transform; x identifies the group and y identifies the RNS limb . The CPU simulator proves the schedule before GPU testing. The current baseline favors exact results over speed; optimization comes next through division-free modular reduction, coalesced data layout, higher radix, and device-resident pipelines. Start here if you haven't: Butterflies all the way down — why the NTT is butterflies at all.

title: 65536: work distribution
summary: Explore the 65536-point forward/inverse polynomial, two-pass blocks, threads, and global access patterns.
text: CUDA execution · a worked example How 65,536 coefficients map to GPU threads. See how our 65536-point forward and inverse NTTs distribute data and butterflies. Start with what a block owns, then zoom into what a thread does. Polynomial → Pass → Block → Thread The whole job The two passes Resources & memory access Forward proof Inverse proof · D3 Row kernels & coverage · D4 Explore a thread Synchronization & RNS 01 Start with the data Consider one polynomial modulo one prime: a[0], a[1], …, a[65535] . Each residue uses 8 bytes, so one RNS limb occupies 512 KiB. 65536 coefficients per modulus 16 stages · 32768 butterflies each 524,288 butterflies · two kernel launches Imagine the same array as 256 rows × 256 columns . This is an index view; the stored array stays flat. global_index = row × 256 + column 02 Divide the work by distance Pass 1 · far stages One block owns one column 32768 → 16384 → 8192 → 4096 → 2048 → 1024 → 512 → 256 These distances preserve the index modulo 256. Each block gathers 256 strided values into shared memory, executes eight stages, and scatters the results back. 256 blocks per modulus. Every block launches 256 threads: 256 load/store values; 128 compute butterflies at each stage. 256 values · 2 KiB shared memory / block Pass 2 · near stages One block owns one row 128 → 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 These butterflies stay inside an aligned 256-value row. Each block loads its contiguous row into shared memory, executes eight stages, and writes it back. 256 blocks per modulus. All 256 threads load/store values; 128 compute butterflies at each stage. 256 values · 2 KiB shared memory / block Both passes use twiddles from the same 65536-point transform . Threads 128–255 still load, store, and reach every barrier, even when they have no butterfly. 03 Resources & memory access The split width is 256: 256 rows × 256 columns . Each column and each row contains 256 values. The algorithm uses two launches, each handling eight stages. Forward schedule per modulus · all blocks launch 256 threads Task / resource N = 65536 Polynomial storage 512 KiB Stages / total butterflies 16 / 524,288 Pass 1 blocks / values per block 256 / 256 Pass 1 shared memory per block 2 KiB Pass 1 loading / butterfly threads 0–255 / 0–127 Pass 1 global distances 32768 down to 256 · 8 stages Pass 2 blocks / values per block 256 / 256 Pass 2 shared memory per block 2 KiB Pass 2 loading / butterfly threads 0–255 / 0–127 Pass 2 global distances 128 down to 1 · 8 stages Pass 1: column 3, thread 5 Block 3 gathers values[3 + 256 × t] into shared[t] , for t = 0…255. Thread 5 loads position 1283. At global distance 32768 (local distance 128), it computes shared positions 5 and 133: global positions 1283 and 34051 . At distance 256 it computes 2563 and 2819 instead. Pass 2: row 3, thread 5 Block 3 loads positions 768…1023. At distance 128, thread 5 computes 773 and 901 ; at distance 1, it computes 778 and 779. The final row, block 255, owns positions 65280…65535. Read the memory access map In pass 1, adjacent loading threads access global addresses 2048 bytes apart (256 × 8 bytes), but write adjacent 8-byte entries in shared memory. The scatter reverses this mapping. In pass 2, adjacent threads read and write adjacent 8-byte global entries. Each block loads once, reuses shared memory across all its stages, and stores once. Two reads and two writes of the value array give a logical minimum of 4 × N × 8 bytes per forward transform: 2 MiB at N=65536, excluding twiddle/modulus reads and host transfers. This is requested array traffic, not measured DRAM traffic . Strided accesses, caches, registers, and occupancy need real-GPU profiling; 128 active butterfly threads out of 256 is not a hardware occupancy measurement. Source map: CUDA kernels and launchers define the grid and gather/scatter; stage helpers map threads to pairs. For N=65536, the gather uses r + 256 × local_index ; near-stage access uses row × 256 + local_index . Within each stage, every position belongs to exactly one butterfly. 04 · D2 Why these inputs and twiddles? Our forward butterfly has two multipliers . Let ψ be the primitive 2N-th root modulo the current prime q. The ladder multiplier is \(c=\psi^d\); the difference-leg multiplier is \(w=\psi^E\). Both are powers from the global transform, not a smaller column NTT. \[a=\mathrm{values}[U],\quad b=\mathrm{values}[V],\qquad x=a+cb,\quad y=(a-cb)w\pmod q.\] The folded twist remains inside every butterfly a b × c × w x y a + cb a − cb \[c=\psi^d,\quad w=\psi^{(N/d)J},\qquad x=a+cb,\quad y=(a-cb)w\pmod q.\] At N=65536, the first column stage has d=32768 and c=ψ³²⁷⁶⁸. At the last column stage d=256, c=ψ²⁵⁶. The row pass continues the same transform with d=128 down to 1. It does not reset ψ or N. How the last two row stages finish the transform Stage (zero-based) d / offset J Factors Outputs 14 2 / 0 or 1 c=ψ²; w=1 or ψ³²⁷⁶⁸ Two size-2 children per size-4 group 15 1 / 0 only c=ψ; w=1 Upper=a+ψb; lower=a−ψb The last layer has no difference-leg multiply by a nontrivial w, but the lower input still carries ψ . Removing c would change the transform to the wrong ring. Final outputs are already in bit-reversed evaluation order. The derivation and full numerical network explain how the original coefficient twist is distributed through these stages. 1. Decode a thread into a local pair The split width B is 256. Column r is blockIdx.x ; p is the butterfly index. At N=65536, each active thread processes just one pair per stage, so p = threadIdx.x . More generally the stage helper loops over p = threadIdx.x + k × blockDim.x . Let δ be the local distance; the global distance is d = B × δ . \[\begin{aligned}g&=\lfloor p/\delta\rfloor,&j&=p\bmod\delta,\\u_{\rm local}&=2\delta g+j,&v_{\rm local}&=u_{\rm local}+\delta,\\U&=B u_{\rm local}+r,&V&=Bv_{\rm local}+r=U+d.\end{aligned}\] 2. Recover the CPU group and offset Substitute the local pair into the global index: \[\begin{aligned}U&=B(2\delta g+j)+r\\&=2dg+(Bj+r),\\\text{group start}&=2dg,\qquad J=Bj+r.\end{aligned}\] Because 0 ≤ j < δ and 0 ≤ r < B , we have 0 ≤ J < Bδ = d . Thus U and V are exactly the CPU pair at offset J in group g. Conversely, every CPU offset has a unique decomposition J = 256j + r . Together with p = gδ + j , this gives one unique column/thread owner for every CPU butterfly. 3. Prove the exponent, not just the result The CPU starts w at 1 for each global group and multiplies it by \(\psi^{N/d}\) after each offset. At offset J it therefore uses \(w=\psi^{(N/d)J}\). Substitution gives: \[c=\psi^d,\qquad E=\frac Nd(256j+r),\qquad w=\psi^E.\] This is precisely the stage helper: if ℓ = log2(δ) , then δ << 8 = d , N >> (8 + ℓ) = N/d , and (j << 8) | r = 256j + r . The OR equals addition because r occupies only the low eight bits. Also 0 ≤ E ≤ N − N/d < N , so the power-table access is in range. A subtle point: thread 0 in column 3 has J = 3, not 0. Its w is generally not 1. Only J = 0 gives exponent 0. The ladder c and w are distinct: the negacyclic ladder remains even when w = 1. 4. Worked pairs at N=65536 All examples use column r = 3. The ladder exponent is d; E is the exponent for the other multiplier. These are indices/exponents, not numeric residues. Swapping those multipliers or omitting either one is incorrect. To recover a and b from just one butterfly, divide both results by 2 modulo q. Why scale only once? Every coefficient traverses log₂N butterflies. Each reversed stage contributes a factor of 2. These factors commute with every stage because the operations are linear modulo q. Thus the entire unnormalized inverse of the forward transform gives 2^(log₂N) × input = N × input . recovered[i] = unnormalized_inverse[i] × N⁻¹ mod q The modulus q is an odd prime and N is a power of two, so N has an inverse modulo q. Our code applies inverse_scale_kernel once at the end, using the inverse length for the selected RNS limb—not floating-point division and not a separate coefficient twist. Reverse the execution, not the array Forward column distances decrease, then forward row distances decrease. The inverse reverses that sequence: row distances increase, then column distances increase, then normalization. Gather/scatter addresses, grid sizes, shared-memory sizes, and active-thread ranges are unchanged for each data subset. Let a=4 and b=5. Forward gives x=15, y=11 . Since w⁻¹=4 and c⁻¹=2, inverse gives t=10, a′=8, b′=10 , exactly 2a and 2b modulo 17. Multiplying by 2⁻¹=9 recovers 4 and 5. This toy example illustrates one butterfly; it is not a column launch for N=8. What the D3 checks establish inverse_column_check executes the real inverse-column helper on CPU. It checks every column pair at N=65536 with tagged tables (262,144 pairs, two basis-input probes each), and every inactive thread. With valid roots for two 46-bit primes, it checks DIT(DIF(stage)) = 2 × input at every column stage and column. They do not compile CUDA, exercise actual launch/barrier behavior, or measure GPU performance. The D4 section below examines contiguous kernels and stage coverage in detail. 06 · D4 Why two passes equal the full transform The column proof handles far stages. The remaining kernels— forward_contiguous_tile_kernel and inverse_contiguous_tile_kernel —assign one contiguous tile to each block. For our target sizes, tile length L is 256; for smaller transforms it is min(256,N) . 1. Map a row thread to the CPU pair Let b be the row block, p the pair index, and d a near-stage distance (128 down to 1 for forward, 1 up to 128 for inverse). Each active thread has p = threadIdx.x for these tiles. \[\begin{aligned}g&=\lfloor p/d\rfloor,\quad j=p\bmod d,\\u_{\rm local}&=2dg+j,\quad v_{\rm local}=u_{\rm local}+d,\\U&=Lb+u_{\rm local},\quad V=U+d,\\\text{group start}&=Lb+2dg,\quad J=j,\quad E=(N/d)j.\end{aligned}\] Why is this a valid CPU group? Since d is a power of two and 2d ≤ L , 2d divides L . Therefore Lb + 2dg is a multiple of 2d, exactly where the CPU group loop begins. Also 0 ≤ j < d and the final local lower index is at most L−1. Every CPU group fits entirely inside an aligned tile. Notice what disappears: the row number b does not appear in J or E. Moving to another aligned row changes the group number, not the offset within that group. But N still appears: these are global-transform powers, not the twiddles of an independent 256-point NTT. \[\begin{aligned}\text{Forward: }&c=\psi^d,\quad w=\psi^{(N/d)j},\\\text{Inverse: }&c^{-1}=(\psi^{-1})^d,\quad w^{-1}=(\psi^{-1})^{(N/d)j}.\end{aligned}\] 2. Trace row 3, thread 5 Row indices and global twiddle exponents at N=65536 d g / j U ↔ V E at N=65536 128 0 / 5 773 ↔ 901 2560 8 0 / 5 773 ↔ 781 40960 1 5 / 0 778 ↔ 779 0 At N=65536, row 255/thread 127/distance 128 reaches the final coefficient: U=65407, V=65535, J=127, E=65024 . Inverse uses the same pairs and reciprocal powers, visited in ascending d order. 3. Account for every stage exactly once The CPU distances are precisely the powers of two from N/2 down to 1. At N≥512, they partition into two disjoint sets: \[\begin{aligned}\text{Far: }&d=32768,16384,\ldots,256,\\\text{Near: }&d=128,64,\ldots,1.\end{aligned}\] Forward runs far distances descending, then near distances descending. Inverse reverses both passes and scales by the inverse of 65536. For other supported N≥512, far distances begin at N/2. There is no missing distance between 128 and 256: no power of two lies between them. Neither set overlaps the other. The far count is log₂N − 8 ; the near count is 8. Each stage has exactly N/2 disjoint butterflies, so the full count is (N/2) × log₂N per direction. Scaling is not an additional butterfly stage. N=65536 · forward and inverse share these stage counts N Far + near stages Total butterflies / direction 65536 8 + 8 = 16 524,288 At N≤256, the far pass is skipped and one tile covers all log₂N stages. The coverage check also exercises N=2, 64, 256 and 512, including the tile clamp and first column-pass boundary. 4. Why block-local stage fusion is safe During all far stages, every dependency stays inside the same column; during all near stages, every dependency stays inside the same tile. A block may therefore finish all its stages before another block finishes its first: those blocks do not consume each other's intermediate values within that pass. This reorders independent operations without changing the CPU result. Each tile loads values[Lb+t] into shared[t] . All threads reach the load barrier and every stage barrier. Threads 0…127 compute butterflies at L=256, while all 256 threads participate in loading/storing and synchronization. The block stores its tile once after the last stage. Within a stage, pair endpoints do not overlap; between stages, the shared-memory barrier makes the preceding writes visible. The dependency rule changes between passes. Results must be scattered before the next pass gathers them; our same-stream kernel sequence provides that boundary. Thus gather/scatter is a change in block ownership, not a transpose or extra arithmetic transform . Together with D2/D3's identical pair arithmetic, exact ordered stage coverage establishes equivalence to the CPU transform. 5. At N=65536 it checks every row, stage and pair in both directions, using two tagged-table input probes per pair, plus inactive-thread checks.
