title: CUDA buffers & dataflow
summary: D5: constructor lifecycle, buffer ownership, host/device copies, fused operations, and integration gaps.
text: CUDA buffers and host/device dataflow — D5 ¶ This is a map of the current implementation, not a proposed device-resident API. Read it alongside the public interface , implementation and launchers , and kernel schedule . The big picture: N=65536, three towers ¶ One CudaNttTransform represents one fixed ring size and a fixed list of RNS moduli/roots. It owns two reusable operand buffers and four constant buffers. The public interface accepts host vectors , not device pointers. For this page, N=65536 and K=3 . One polynomial contains 196,608 64-bit residues: 1,572,864 bytes (1.5 MiB) . Each tower occupies 512 KiB. ① Construct once Allocate six GPU buffers: 6,291,552 B total. Upload four constant arrays: 3,145,824 B, four copies. ② Reuse for each call Host inputs → GPU A/B → kernels → host result. A and B are each 1.5 MiB. Constants stay on the GPU. ③ Destroy Free all six allocations after successful construction. CPU vectors and GPU allocations have separate ownership. Constants and scratch allocations persist across calls. Operand contents are scratch state and are overwritten by the next call. Only the internal chain inside multiply() remains device-resident between its arithmetic operations. Calling public forward() , pointwise_multiply() , and inverse() separately does not preserve a transfer-free pipeline. Constructor: what happens, in order ¶ Allocate Impl with new Impl{} ; all six CUDA pointers start as null. Reject empty moduli or a moduli/root count mismatch. Store N and limb count K. Set tile length min(256,N) and column length N/256 . For every limb, construct a NegacyclicNtt CPU reference and build powers of ψ and ψ-inverse for exponents 0 through N inclusive . Compute N-inverse. Allocate the six persistent CUDA buffers listed below. Host allocations have already occurred; parameter checks precede device allocation. Upload both power tables, the moduli, and inverse lengths: four H2D copies. Record row-grid count max(1,N/256) and elementwise-grid count ceil(K*N/256) . All kernels launch 256 threads per block. The CPU constructor checks power-of-two N≥2, (q−1) % (2N) == 0 , ψ^N mod q == q−1 , and q>N. It assumes prime q; it does not itself run a primality test. The parameter generator is a separate source of checked primes. See parameter generation . After construction, temporary host power-table/inverse-length vectors are released. Impl retains the moduli vector and per-limb CPU references, not a second permanent host copy of every power table. Persistent allocation and ownership map ¶ For N=65536/K=3, define S=1,572,864 B, T=1,572,888 B, R=24 B. In general, \(S=8KN,\ T=8K(N+1),\ R=8K\) bytes. Every stored element is uint64_t . Device allocation Elements / bytes Layout and role Writer / reader device_operand_a 196,608 / 1,572,864 B [limb][coefficient or evaluation position] ; working input/output Public input copy and kernels write; result copy reads device_operand_b 196,608 / 1,572,864 B Second operand; separate from A Input copy and its forward transform write; pointwise kernel reads device_twiddle_powers 196,611 / 1,572,888 B [limb][exponent] , \(\psi^e\) Constructor uploads; forward kernels read device_inverse_twiddle_powers 196,611 / 1,572,888 B [limb][exponent] , \((\psi^{-1})^e\) Constructor uploads; inverse kernels read device_moduli 3 / 24 B q for each limb Constructor uploads; arithmetic kernels read device_inverse_transform_lengths 3 / 24 B N-inverse modulo each q Constructor uploads; final scale kernel reads CudaNttTransform owns Impl* ; Impl owns the CUDA pointers. They are private: callers cannot retain a borrowed device-buffer view. Copy construction and copy assignment are deleted. No move operations are declared; this class is not currently movable either. Do not use one instance concurrently: public operations share and overwrite A/B and there is no locking or per-call scratch. On normal destruction, ~CudaNttTransform() deletes Impl , whose destructor calls cudaFree on each pointer. Free errors are deliberately ignored. Do not infer safe concurrent destruction or synchronization with unrelated GPU work. Exact byte counts (requested allocations, not measured device usage) ¶ \[ \begin{aligned} \text{Operands}&=2S=3{,}145{,}728\ \mathrm{B},\\ \text{Constants}&=2T+2R=3{,}145{,}824\ \mathrm{B},\\ \text{All six}&=2S+2T+2R=6{,}291{,}552\ \mathrm{B}. \end{aligned} \] For three limbs , the source formulas give: N One operand S Both operands Constants / constructor upload All six allocations 65536 1,572,864 B (1.5 MiB) 3,145,728 B 3,145,824 B 6,291,552 B The extra 96 bytes comprise 48 bytes for the two power tables' final entries and 48 bytes for the moduli and inverse lengths. CUDA context/allocator overhead, registers, per-block shared memory, host vectors, and CPU-reference objects are not included. These are formulas, not a VRAM measurement or a memory-capacity benchmark. Public API contracts ¶ For operands, flat index k*N+i belongs to limb k. Power-table index k*(N+1)+e belongs to exponent e of that limb. Transform kernels select limbs with blockIdx.y . Pointwise and scale kernels instead use a flat grid over K*N entries and recover the limb by integer division by N. Public call Input → output representation Host-visible effect Copies / launches at N≥512 forward(values) Natural coefficients → bit-reversed evaluations Mutates host vector H2D A, column + row, D2H A: 2 copies, 2 launches inverse(values) Bit-reversed evaluations → natural coefficients Mutates host vector H2D A, row + column + scale, D2H A: 2 copies, 3 launches pointwise_multiply(left,right) Matching bit-reversed evaluations → same order Replaces left; right is a const input H2D A+B, pointwise, D2H A: 3 copies, 1 launch multiply(left,right) Natural coefficients → natural negacyclic product Left is passed by value; returns its result buffer H2D A+B, 2 forwards + pointwise + inverse, D2H A: 3 copies, 8 launches Inputs must contain K*N residues in their corresponding [0,q[k]) ranges. Methods check lengths, but do not scan residue ranges or store a runtime coefficient/evaluation tag. The caller is responsible for representation and parameter compatibility. A vector from another modulus set with the same length is not rejected merely for having different provenance. n() and limbs() return scalar geometry without a device copy. q(k) and ref(k) use bounds-checked host vectors; ref(k) is a borrowed const reference valid only while the transform object exists. These getters do not expose the GPU allocation or transfer data. Follow a complete multiplication ¶ HOST · input left: 196,608 residues right: 196,608 residues ↓ H2D · 2 copies · 3 MiB total GPU · reusable A and B A · 1.5 MiB Coefficients ↓ column DIF · 256 blocks/tower ↓ row DIF · 256 blocks/tower Bit-reversed evaluations B · 1.5 MiB Coefficients ↓ column DIF · 256 blocks/tower ↓ row DIF · 256 blocks/tower Bit-reversed evaluations ↓ A × B, write A · 1 kernel · 768 blocks A · product evaluations ↓ row DIT → column DIT → inverse scale 3 kernels; result: 196,608 coefficient residues Constants stay here: forward powers 1,572,888 B + inverse powers 1,572,888 B + moduli 24 B + inverse lengths 24 B. ↓ D2H · 1 copy · 1.5 MiB HOST · returned left 196,608 residues · 1.5 MiB · natural coefficient order For this three-tower example, each transform launch has a 256×3 grid, 256 threads per block, and 2 KiB shared memory per block. The pointwise and scale grids each have 768 blocks. A complete multiply uses eight launches and three operand copies, totaling 4,718,592 B (4.5 MiB) . The four constant buffers are read throughout this chain; they are not re-uploaded per operation. B is scratch after the call, not a cached operand that the next public operation is entitled to reuse. Every new multiply() uploads both input operands again. Passing an lvalue as left creates a host copy; passing a moved vector can transfer its host allocation into the by-value parameter instead. Each public method uses cudaMemcpy , not cudaMemcpyAsync , and returns the downloaded host result. Launches specify no explicit stream; there is no public stream/event parameter, asynchronous completion handle, or device-resident buffer API. cudaGetLastError() follows launches; copies are also checked by CHECK_CUDA . There is no automatic CPU fallback on a CUDA error. Transfer boundary: fused versus separate calls ¶ Excluding construction, each forward/inverse transfers 2S bytes and pointwise or fused multiply transfers 3S bytes. For a fair comparison of two inputs : Route for two input polynomials Copies Requested transfer payload Kernel launches Four public calls: forward A, forward B, pointwise, inverse 9 14,155,776 B (13.5 MiB) 8 One multiply(A,B) call 3 4,718,592 B (4.5 MiB) 8 Both paths perform eight kernels at the target sizes. Fusion removes six operand-sized transfer copies (9S→3S), not six kernels. At N=65536/K=3 this is 14,155,776 B versus 4,718,592 B of requested H2D+D2H payload. It is not a measured latency speedup. Host vector copies, allocator costs and PCIe/cache effects are separate. At N≤256 forward uses one kernel, inverse two and multiply five; the host-copy counts are unchanged. The benchmark wraps public calls in wall-clock timing, so its GPU columns include operand transfers. Construction/table uploads occur outside that per-call region; see run_bench in the implementation. It is not kernel-only timing. Open ownership and integration issues ¶ Constructor exception cleanup: impl_ is a raw pointer initialized with new Impl{} . If the constructor subsequently throws, the enclosing object's destructor is not run and nothing in the constructor deletes that pointer. Invalid parameters can leak host state; allocation/upload failure can also leak previously allocated CUDA buffers. This is a source-inspected cleanup gap, not a fault-injection result. Introduce RAII in a dedicated implementation change and verify allocation/upload failure paths before production use. No device identifier is captured in the object and no device guard is used around operations/destruction. Multi-device ownership is not specified. No stream/event lifetime contract, buffer view, representation/level tag, evaluation-key cache, or OpenFHE Q/P base-switch integration exists in this interface. Reusable allocations are not the final integration API. Native CUDA compilation and launch/barrier behavior are still unverified here. CPU schedule tests do not compile or run this CUDA wrapper. D9 should freeze these ownership/API decisions; the production device API and RAII implementation must follow explicit failure/lifetime tests. The D6 arithmetic review examines arithmetic bounds, parameter assumptions, and adversarial exactness. Verification and limits ¶ Source-contract tests check that this map matches current allocation sizes, frees, public copy directions, operation ordering and host-only interface shape. They also pin the N=65536 arithmetic above. These are deliberately static source checks , not CUDA-runtime tests or proof of constructor failure safety. Existing CTests verify CPU arithmetic and shared stage helpers. No new claim of actual GPU support/performance is made by completing D5.

title: Arithmetic bounds & tests
summary: D6: canonical residues, overflow proofs, bigint checks, full-size adversarial cases, and remaining exactness gates.
text: Modular arithmetic: bounds and exactness gates ¶ D6 connects the butterfly formulas to the integer operations they actually execute. The current target is N=65536, with 50–60-bit prime towers stored in uint64_t . This is a correctness contract, not a GPU performance result. Read the buffer/dataflow map first for where the arrays live. The implementation is in mod_arith.hpp , ntt.hpp , and dev_core.hpp . 1. What callers must supply ¶ Canonical means an integer in \([0,q)\) . None of the hot arithmetic functions validates this range at runtime. Operation Required input Output add_mod(a,b,q) Canonical a,b; \(0<q<2^{63}\) Canonical \((a+b)\bmod q\) sub_mod(a,b,q) Canonical a,b; \(0<q<2^{63}\) Canonical \((a-b)\bmod q\) mul_mod(a,b,q) Canonical a,b; \(0<q<2^{64}\) Canonical \(ab\bmod q\) pow_mod(a,e,q) Any uint64_t a,e; q>0 Canonical \(a^e\bmod q\) ; q=1 returns 0 inv_mod(x,q) Prime q≥2; x not divisible by q Canonical inverse via \(x^{q-2}\) Add/sub retain their documented conservative bound; this review does not expand the public contract. Multiplication's wider bound does not make a full transform with q≥2^63 part of the supported contract. For a transform, also require a power-of-two N≥2, prime q with \(2N\mid(q-1)\) , and the same primitive 2N-th root ψ as the comparison implementation. At the target N, \(2N=131072\) and q>N. Forward consumes canonical coefficients in natural order; inverse consumes canonical evaluations in bit-reversed order. There is no Montgomery representation or lazy residue format in this code. The constructor checks size shape, divisibility and \(\psi^N=q-1\) , but does not test primality or the advertised modulus-width limit . Public array methods check length, not residue bounds. Trusted parameter selection and canonical input are caller obligations today, not rejection guarantees. 2. Why intermediates fit ¶ For canonical a,b: Addition: \(0\le a+b\le 2q-2\) . One subtraction is sufficient. The code forms the sum in 128 bits; after subtraction it is below q and fits uint64_t. Subtraction: if a≥b, use a-b. Otherwise \(0\le a+(q-b)<q\) ; the selected branch therefore cannot overflow uint64_t. Do not compute unsigned a-b first and assume wraparound implements reduction modulo q. Multiplication: \(0\le ab\le(q-1)^2<2^{128}\) . The cast happens before multiplication, preserving the full product; remainder produces a value below q. Multiplying in uint64_t first would lose the high half. At q<2^60, the product is below 2^120 and a sum below 2^61. Storage in uint64_t is safe, but a uint64_t product is still insufficient. Exponentiation reduces a before its first multiply. Each multiplication preserves canonical range. A uint64_t exponent takes at most 64 loop iterations. Even e=0 computes 1 % q , so q=0 is never legal. These are bounds for the current exact-remainder code. Barrett, Shoup, Montgomery, 32-bit limbs, or lazy reduction will need their own proofs, including quotient error, carries, temporary width, and final correction. 3. The invariant through every butterfly ¶ Forward and inverse use these canonical modular operations: \[ \begin{aligned} \text{Forward: }&t=cv\bmod q,\quad u'=u+t\bmod q,\quad v'=(u-t)w\bmod q,\\ \text{Inverse: }&t=yw^{-1}\bmod q,\quad u'=x+t\bmod q,\quad v'=(x-t)c^{-1}\bmod q. \end{aligned} \] Tables contain canonical powers. Every operation above returns canonical values, so induction over all 16 stages preserves \([0,q)\) . Inverse's final multiplication by N-inverse does too. Pointwise multiplication has the same invariant. There is no stage where values are intentionally in \([0,2q)\) or \([0,4q)\) . Feeding lazy OpenFHE/internal buffers directly into this interface without an explicit representation contract would violate its assumptions. What arithmetic work is actually counted ¶ N=65536 has \(32768\times16=524288\) butterflies per direction and per tower. The CPU reference uses three modular multiplications per butterfly: two for data and one to advance the twiddle. Shared device-stage helpers use two, reading precomputed twiddles instead. Thus the loop bodies perform 1,572,864 and 1,048,576 multiplications respectively; inverse adds 65,536 normalization multiplies. Setup powers/table generation are additional work. The old arithmetic-header comment counted the CPU loop incorrectly; D6 fixes that comment without changing the algorithms. __uint128_t remainder is the correctness baseline. Its CUDA lowering and cost must be checked in a native build/profile, not inferred as one hardware division instruction. 4. Executable adversarial coverage ¶ Two new gates run in the normal CPU CTest suite: Gate Inputs and comparison What it establishes arithmetic_bigint_check 14,956 compiled results versus Python arbitrary-precision addition, subtraction, multiplication, power and modular inverse Exact host primitive answers, not a copy of the same C++ reduction expression arithmetic_transform_check N=65536 at generated 50-, 55-, 60-bit primes; six patterns in both coefficient/evaluation roundtrips Canonical forward/inverse results and two-sided roundtrip identity Same transform gate \(x^{N-1}\cdot x\) must produce q-1 at index 0 and zero elsewhere Closed-form negacyclic wrap sign, not merely roundtrip consistency Primitive inputs include 0, 1, 2, q/2, q-2, q-1, values around 2^32, and 256 seeded random pairs per modulus. Moduli include small, even, composite, 50/55/60-bit boundaries, just below 2^63, and full-width uint64_t boundaries. The latter use mul/pow only, respecting the add/sub contract. Exponents include 0, 1, 2, 63, 64 and UINT64_MAX; pow also receives an unreduced base. Inverse checks small and generated 50/55/60-bit primes against Python's modular-inverse algorithm, and confirms the host exception for zero/multiples of q. Parameter generation is reused; this is not an independent primality certification test. The six transform patterns are zero, all q-1, alternating zero/q-1, a final coefficient impulse, ramp and deterministic pseudorandom. A roundtrip alone cannot prove spectral ordering or OpenFHE compatibility; use the other gates. cmake -S . -B build cmake --build build -j 8 ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure ctest --test-dir build -R 'arithmetic_' -V Sources: C++ probe and full-size tests , independent primitive oracle . 5. Exactness ladder: do not substitute one gate for another ¶ Existing gate Scope Limit unit_tests Small arithmetic and NTT product against schoolbook Schoolbook shares arithmetic primitives oracle_crosscheck N=1024 forward arrays against direct Python NTT sum, plus CRT and identity Not a full-size GPU test Column/inverse/tile mapping checks Exhaustive target-size index/twiddle probes of shared CPU/CUDA helpers CPU execution; no CUDA barriers/races tested device_schedule_check Exact simulator/reference arrays, including N=65536 fixtures Current fixtures use 46-bit primes openfhe_exact_compat (opt-in) N=65536 NativePoly forward/inverse arrays, including independent evaluation input; OpenFHE selects parameters via FirstPrime(50) and LastPrime(59) Pinned OpenFHE 1.6.1 CPU comparison, not a CUDA/OpenFHE pipeline Native CUDA oracle/reference gates (when CUDA is available) Actual kernel outputs versus reference/oracle Must be run on named hardware; not verified on this Mac The OpenFHE gate includes zero, all q-1, ramp, random coefficients and random evaluation arrays. Same q and root are essential: another valid root may give a different evaluation permutation. The D7 contract freezes the representation and tower boundary. CKKS approximate decryption is not a replacement for these exact per-index comparisons. 6. Deferred adversarial checks and unsafe inputs ¶ D6's review is complete; these are explicit later implementation gates: P2/P3, real GPU: repeat the 50/55/60-bit patterns through actual kernels, compare each forward/inverse/pointwise result and canonical range, then run compute-sanitizer race/memory checks and test launch failures. CPU success does not establish nvcc support, device reduction correctness, or timing. D9/API hardening: define rejection policy for noncanonical residues, incompatible roots, composite moduli, zero/oversized dimensions, and mismatched vector/tower metadata. Add negative tests when those contracts are implemented; do not claim current APIs reject all invalid inputs. Parameter helpers: find_primes currently assumes safe shifts and a nonzero, nonoverflowing 2N . Invalid bit counts can cause undefined shifts; find_psi assumes a compatible prime q>3 and has no attempt limit. These helpers are not hardened untrusted-input parsers. Raw primitive misuse: q=0 causes invalid remainder/division operations; it is not a test input to execute. Composite q violates Fermat inverse's premise even if x is invertible: for example q=15,x=2 returns 2, not 8. Host zero-input inverse throws; the device branch returns 0 and is not a supported inverse/error-reporting API. Device kernels currently never invert. Future reduction optimization: exercise maximum correction counts, carry/borrow transitions, high-word products and every accepted lazy range against the independent bigint gate before allowing an optimized dispatch. These gaps do not block the D6 source-review deliverable. They do block claims of a hardened production API or GPU/OpenFHE integration. P1 remains open; the D8 Hybrid graph is complete. The next deliverable is D9: device buffer, stream, and cache contracts .

title: OpenFHE representation
summary: D7: exact coefficient/evaluation ordering, root selection, DCRT tower packing, format APIs, and executable compatibility checks.
text: OpenFHE representation contract — D7 ¶ This freezes the NTT/DCRT boundary for OpenFHE 1.6.1 , commit b59e1f291965f14fbee5172cd83a20f5b856204f , at N=65536 . This contract uses the 64-bit NativeInteger backend . It covers coefficient/evaluation format, exact array order, per-tower parameters, and packing into the current CUDA interface. The D8 Hybrid operation graph builds on this boundary. The executable evidence is openfhe_representation_tests.cpp . It uses the real OpenFHE core library on CPU. No native CUDA result is claimed. 1. The boundary in one table ¶ Property Required contract Ring \(\mathbb Z_q[x]/(x^N+1)\) , \(N=65536\) ; cyclotomic order \(m=2N=131072\) Coefficient index i Coefficient of \(x^i\) , in natural order Evaluation memory index k Evaluation at \(\psi^{2\operatorname{rev}_{16}(k)+1}\) , with 16-bit index reversal Tower modulus q The exact modulus in that tower's OpenFHE parameters Root ψ The exact primitive 2N-th root in those same parameters Residue representation Unsigned canonical values in \([0,q)\) ; no external twist or Montgomery conversion Forward Natural coefficients → bit-reversed evaluations, in place Inverse Bit-reversed evaluations → natural coefficients; N-inverse normalization included GPU buffer order values[limb*N + index] , preserving the supplied tower list These evaluation indices are not CKKS's decoded complex-slot indices . Encoding/decoding uses another embedding and is outside this NTT contract. 2. What each format means ¶ OpenFHE's Format enum names COEFFICIENT and EVALUATION . The label alone does not express index ordering. For the power-of-two ring, NativePoly::SwitchFormat calls ForwardTransformToBitReverseInPlace or InverseTransformFromBitReverseInPlace . The NTT's evaluation array is therefore bit-reversed even though its public format is simply EVALUATION . Our reference and CUDA entry points do not store an OpenFHE format flag. The caller must know the current domain before invoking forward() or inverse() . Calling forward twice is not an idempotent format assignment. No explicit input twist or output permutation is needed at this boundary. The negacyclic twist is already folded into the butterfly schedule. Ordinary bit reversal changes an index , not byte order or the bits of a residue. 3. Exact evaluation and inverse formulas ¶ Let rev16(k) reverse the low 16 bits of k and define \(r_k=\psi^{2\operatorname{rev}_{16}(k)+1}\pmod q\) . Then: \[ \mathrm{forward}(a)[k]=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}a_i r_k^i\pmod q, \qquad \mathrm{inverse}(y)[i]=N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}y_k r_k^{-i}\pmod q. \] The first natural evaluation indices in memory are 0, 32768, 16384, 49152, 8192, ... . Thus the corresponding root exponents begin 1, 65537, 32769, 98305, 16385, ... . In particular, slot 0 contains \(a(\psi)\) and slot 1 contains \(a(-\psi)\) . Probe Expected array \(a(x)=1\) Every evaluation is 1 \(a(x)=x\) Slot k is \(r_k\) \(a(x)=x^{17}\) Slot k is \(r_k^{17}\) \(a(x)=x^{N-1}\) Slot k is \(r_k^{N-1}\) Evaluation array with 1 only at slot s Coefficient i is \(N^{-1}r_s^{-i}\) These closed forms distinguish order and scaling errors that a shared forward/inverse round trip could conceal. The D7 gate checks all N outputs, not just the first few slots. 4. Changing format versus changing its label ¶ The shared SetFormat implementation calls SwitchFormat only when the requested format differs from the current one. API Effect SetFormat(current_format) No conversion; values remain unchanged SetFormat(other_format) Runs the forward or inverse transform SwitchFormat() Always toggles format and transforms values NativePoly::SetValues(values, format) Assigns the values and label; does not transform them NativePoly::OverrideFormat(format) Changes only the label DCRTPoly::OverrideFormat(format) Changes only the outer label; does not retag or transform its NativePoly children The last two methods are not substitutes for conversion. A DCRT object with outer EVALUATION and coefficient-format children is inconsistent. Keep the outer and child formats aligned when importing GPU results. To import an already-transformed array, create an evaluation-format NativePoly for each tower and assign its values with the evaluation label. Inverting it again during import would undo the GPU computation. D7 tests this import path using a separate DCRT object. 5. Roots, prime widths, and the transform cache ¶ A valid primitive root is not necessarily the same root. Replacing ψ by \(\psi^3\) still gives a primitive 2N-th root but changes the evaluation addresses. Do not regenerate roots using this repository's independent parameter finder when comparing or importing an OpenFHE context. Read each tower's root. The pinned RootOfUnity implementation chooses the smallest primitive root by enumerating primitive powers. The D7 fixtures use this function with LastPrime(bits, 2N) for exact 50-, 55-, and 60-bit primes. The test independently enumerates odd root powers and checks the minimum. FirstPrime(bits, m) searches above \(2^{\mathrm{bits}}\) ; its argument is not a guarantee of a prime with exactly that many bits. LastPrime searches below that bound and checks the resulting bit length. This is why the D7 matrix uses LastPrime. Cache constraint: the pinned FTT table cache looks up by modulus and checks table length; it does not compare the requested root on a cache hit. Use a consistent root for each modulus/ring-size pair. The gate tests the normal OpenFHE-generated root choice. Arbitrary custom-root contexts sharing a modulus are not covered by this result. Do not call a global cache reset inside an integration adapter to work around this constraint. OpenFHE's bit-reversed power tables and preconditioned multiplication constants are internal implementation data. They are not interchangeable with this repository's \([\psi^0,\ldots,\psi^N]\) table. Share parameter values and polynomial arrays; construct backend-specific twiddle tables separately. 6. DCRT tower order and flat GPU packing ¶ DCRTPoly owns a vector of NativePoly objects. Each tower has its own modulus, root, format, and value allocation. The ILDCRTParams constructor retains the provided modulus/root order and forms the composite modulus Q as their product. The polynomial's composite Q can exceed 64 bits. It is not a native tower modulus and must not be truncated into the CUDA modulus array. For N=65536, each row below is copied from its own NativePoly allocation: OpenFHE tower Parameters Flat GPU element range Byte offset 0 \((q_0,\psi_0)\) 0…65535 0 1 \((q_1,\psi_1)\) 65536…131071 524288 2 \((q_2,\psi_2)\) 131072…196607 1048576 \[ \mathrm{address}(\ell,i)=65536\ell+i,\qquad Q=q_0q_1q_2. \] Read the active tower list from the object, not a hard-coded sorted list or an assumed CKKS level. The D7 test deliberately uses bit widths in the order 55, 50, 60 so sorting or swapping towers cannot silently pass. Packing coefficient data requires \(a_i\bmod q_\ell\) at each address. For an integer coefficient -1, this is \(q_\ell-1\) in every tower. The test starts from a BigInteger polynomial containing \(Q-1\) and \(2^{64}+17\) , imports it as a DCRTPoly, and checks all residues and coefficient-domain CRT reconstruction. No interpolation is needed to run the per-tower NTT itself. CRTInterpolate() requires coefficient format and returns a BigInteger Poly with the placeholder root 1. That root is not a valid primitive 2N-th root; do not use the interpolated object's placeholder to configure an NTT backend. OpenFHE's separate tower allocations are not one contiguous host buffer. Copy values tower by tower into the flat buffer; do not reinterpret-cast the DCRT object or assume its NativeInteger objects have the GPU's scalar ABI. The D5 dataflow map describes the current host-vector API and the ownership/stream work still required for D9. 7. Pointwise products and active levels ¶ With matching q, ψ, format, and slot order, pointwise evaluation multiplication followed by inverse gives the negacyclic ring product. D7 multiplies a full three-tower DCRT polynomial by x and checks the independent coefficient rule: \[ \mathrm{out}_i= \begin{cases} -\mathrm{in}_{N-1}\pmod q,&i=0,\\ \mathrm{in}_{i-1},&1\le i<N. \end{cases} \] Both the wrap term and large-input coefficient residues are checked. DropLastElement() removes the last tower and its parameter. It retains the remaining ordered prefix without scaling or transforming values. It is not CKKS rescaling, ModUp, or ModDown. D7 checks this prefix behavior, including that dropping a copied object's last tower does not change the original's parameter list. The D8 graph records the actual Hybrid basis and reduction operations. 8. Adapter checklist and remaining scope ¶ Before handing an object to the backend: Check N and cyclotomic order, then obtain the actual ordered active towers. Retain each tower's q and ψ; validate the supported modulus/root contract. Establish the domain and ordering, with consistent outer/child formats. Pack canonical values at limb*N+index , without a twist or permutation. Run the explicitly requested operation. Inverse includes normalization. Import results with matching parameters and truthful format labels. This freezes the power-of-two NTT and DCRT array boundary. It does not freeze Hybrid digit order, Q/P concatenation, rounding, key layout, device ownership, stream/event lifetime, or CPU fallback. The D8 graph now specifies Hybrid digit order, Q/P layout, and the pinned CKKS reduction sequence; device ownership and the integration API remain D9–D10 deliverables. The P1 architecture exit gate remains open. 9. Run the checks ¶ After installing the pinned OpenFHE release with scripts/openfhe_setup.sh : cmake -S . -B build/openfhe-compat/ntt-build \ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DNTT_ENABLE_OPENFHE_COMPAT=ON \ -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$PWD/build/openfhe-compat/install" cmake --build build/openfhe-compat/ntt-build -j ctest --test-dir build/openfhe-compat/ntt-build \ -R 'openfhe_exact_compat|openfhe_representation_contract' --output-on-failure The original gate retains random and boundary coefficient cases plus an independent inverse input. The new representation gate adds full-size monomial and inverse-basis formulas, format API behavior, root selection, three-tower packing/import, BigInteger coefficients, pointwise multiplication, and tower dropping. It links only OpenFHE core. See the daily entry for observed build and publication results. Pinned source references ¶ All links below identify the exact OpenFHE commit inspected for this contract. The linked entry points lead to the statements used above. Format enum and SetFormat . NativePoly SwitchFormat and SetValues . FTT dispatch and cached tables . RootOfUnity and prime selection . DCRT format conversion and tower parameters . DCRT interpolation and dropping a tower .

title: Hybrid operation graph
summary: D8: exact digit extension, Q/P tower addressing, key MAC, ModDown, delayed operations, and full-size OpenFHE checks.
text: OpenFHE Hybrid key switching: the exact operation graph ¶ D8 traces OpenFHE 1.6.1 , commit b59e1f291965f14fbee5172cd83a20f5b856204f , with N=65536 and the 64-bit NativeInteger backend. It fixes the sequence of representation changes, CRT representatives, key addressing, accumulation, and reduction that a future backend must preserve. Read the D7 representation contract for the NTT's exact array order. The executable evidence is openfhe_hybrid_tests.cpp . It calls the actual OpenFHE PKE library and compares complete arrays with an independent unreduced-CRT formula and scalar arithmetic. These are CPU results. 1. Read the complete path ¶ The ordinary path starts at KeySwitchCore(c,key) . Its output is two contributions in the active Q basis, ordered B first, A second . The ciphertext wrapper decides how to combine them with existing components. Split the active Q towers Contiguous groups of up to α towers form the digits. Keep their original evaluation arrays. Convert each digit to coefficients Inverse NTT only the towers in that digit. Extend to its complement Approximate CRT produces coefficients in every other active Q tower and every P tower. Return the complement to evaluations Forward NTT those new towers, then stitch them around the saved original digit towers. Multiply and accumulate in QlP All digits contribute to two evaluation arrays, using the B and A key vectors. Reduce each accumulated result Inverse NTT its P towers, approximate-switch P to active Q, forward NTT the correction, subtract, and multiply by the inverse of P. Update the ciphertext Add the first contribution to c0; add or replace c1 according to the caller. The implementation has no general coefficient-domain round trip of all QlP towers. It preserves the original digit evaluations during extension and leaves Q evaluations intact during ModDown. 2. Names, levels, and tower order ¶ Let M be the full context's Q-tower count, L the current ciphertext's active Q-tower count, K the P-tower count, and D the configured large-digit count. The active basis is an ordered prefix of Q: \[ Q_\ell=\prod_{i=0}^{L-1}q_i,\qquad P=\prod_{j=0}^{K-1}p_j,\qquad \alpha=\left\lceil\frac{M}{D}\right\rceil,\qquad \beta_\ell=\left\lceil\frac{L}{\alpha}\right\rceil. \] The source also caps the active digit count at the configured partition count. For valid active prefixes this does not alter the formula above. α belongs to the full context; do not recompute it from L. The last active digit may be shorter than α, including when only part of the first digit remains. Object Tower order Representation Input component q₀ … qₗ₋₁ Evaluation, bit-reversed within each tower Digit d's source q at indices dα … min((d+1)α,L)−1 Evaluation, then coefficient Digit d's complement Other active Q towers in order, then p₀ … pₖ₋₁ Coefficient, then evaluation Assembled digit Active Q prefix, then all P Evaluation Stored key pair for digit d Full Q, then all P Evaluation Each MAC output Active Q prefix, then all P Evaluation Each ModDown output Active Q prefix Evaluation Here L is a tower count , not the ciphertext's public GetLevel() value. Derive it from the actual element parameters; D9 must keep these metadata consistent. Every tower retains its exact OpenFHE modulus and root. 3. Why approximate CRT must keep the unreduced sum ¶ For a digit's actual source basis \(B=\prod_i b_i\) , define \(\widehat B_i=B/b_i\) . At coefficient index r, the implementation computes: \[ t_i=[x_i\widehat B_i^{-1}]_{b_i},\qquad S=\sum_i t_i\widehat B_i,\qquad \widetilde x_m=[S]_m. \] Brackets mean the canonical residue in the indicated modulus. The final modulus m is a complement tower. There is no reduction of S modulo B before reducing it modulo m. In general: \[ S=x+\kappa B,\qquad 0\le x<B,\qquad [S]_m\ne[x]_m. \] ApproxSwitchCRTBasis implements this sum using the precomputed hat inverses, hat residues, and modular multiplication/accumulation. Our test independently forms the full unreduced sum with arbitrary-precision BigInteger arithmetic; it does not read those conversion tables to compute its expected answer. The digit is converted to coefficient format before this operation. Its complement is then transformed using each destination tower's own root. The digit's original evaluation towers are copied directly into their slots. Applying the CRT formula to evaluation coordinates would change the result. This contract uses WITH_REDUCED_NOISE=OFF . The centered-conversion branch selected by that build option is different and is outside this fixture matrix. 4. A reduced level changes key addresses ¶ A key keeps all M Q towers followed by K P towers. A ciphertext digit contains only L Q towers followed by those same K P towers. For active-array index i: \[ \operatorname{keyIndex}(i)= \begin{cases} i,&i<L,\\ i+(M-L),&i\ge L. \end{cases} \] For the fixture M=5, α=3, K=3 , reducing to L=4 gives: Array Tower positions Active digit q₀, q₁, q₂, q₃, p₀, p₁, p₂ Full key indices used 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 Full key index skipped 4, the dropped q₄ Index 4 in the active digit is p₀, while index 4 in the key is q₄. Using the same flat index for both silently reads the wrong key tower when unchecked multiplication is used. The diagnostic key gives every digit, tower, and evaluation position a distinct deterministic value to expose this. Explore the active level Choose the number of remaining Q towers in the executable fixture. 5 Q towers 4 Q towers 3 Q towers 2 Q towers 1 Q tower 5. Two MACs, then two ModDowns ¶ For digit evaluation array d and key arrays A and B, each active tower m and bit-reversed evaluation coordinate k compute: \[ Z_{0,m,k}=\left[\sum_d D_{d,m,k}B_{d,\operatorname{keyIndex}(m),k}\right]_m, \] \[ Z_{1,m,k}=\left[\sum_d D_{d,m,k}A_{d,\operatorname{keyIndex}(m),k}\right]_m. \] EvalFastKeySwitchCoreExt returns these two QlP arrays. The multiplication is pointwise; there is no NTT inside the MAC loop. All products and sums remain canonical residues. The evaluation key already supplies the gadget scaling: in private-to-private generation, its old-secret term is P times the old secret on that digit's Q towers, and zero on its other towers. Do not add an extra global twist or a guessed CRT/gadget multiplier to the digits. For each accumulated array Z, extract and inverse-transform its P towers: \[ u_j=\operatorname{INTT}_{p_j}(Z_{p_j}),\qquad \widehat P_j=P/p_j, \] \[ R_i=\left[\sum_j [u_j\widehat P_j^{-1}]_{p_j}\widehat P_j\right]_{q_i}, \] \[ Y_{q_i}=\left[(Z_{q_i}-\operatorname{NTT}_{q_i}(R_i)) [P^{-1}]_{q_i}\right]_{q_i}. \] This is the exact implementation order for the pinned CKKS path. Its noise scale is 1, so the source passes t=0 and skips the BGV-specific t factors. There is no floating-point rounding operation in these steps. Calling this “division by P” does not authorize replacing its approximate representative with a canonical or centered CRT representative, or with a generic rounding rule. Accumulate before ModDown. Moving ModDown inside the digit sum changes carry/correction terms. A simple scalar illustration with q=97 and P=17 is \(\operatorname{Down}(16)=0\) , \(\operatorname{Down}(1)=0\) , but \(\operatorname{Down}(17)=1\) . This is a modular-arithmetic example, not a small polynomial fixture. The full-size test also explicitly checks that the wrong per-digit reduction order produces different arrays. 6. Which wrapper calls which graph? ¶ Entry point Result and caller obligation EvalKeySwitchPrecomputeCore β active digit arrays in QlP; reusable for hoisted operations with compatible parameters EvalFastKeySwitchCoreExt Two QlP MAC arrays; reduction is deferred EvalFastKeySwitchCore Extended MAC followed by ModDown of both arrays KeySwitchCore Precompute followed by the fast core; two Q contributions KeySwitchInPlace with two components Add B contribution to c₀; replace c₁ with the A contribution KeySwitchInPlace with three components Add B to c₀ and A to c₁; discard c₂ Relinearization Switch each component from index 2 using the corresponding evaluation key, accumulate into c₀/c₁, then resize to two For the in-place wrapper: \[ c'_0=c_0+Y_0,\qquad c'_1=\begin{cases}Y_1,&\text{two-component input},\\c_1+Y_1,&\text{three-component input}.\end{cases} \] D8 executes the two- and three-component wrapper cases. The source trace also records the general relinearization loop; higher ciphertext degrees and their full key families remain a later integration test. Delayed QP operations are distinct from digit extension ¶ KeySwitchExt(ciphertext,addFirst) multiplies the retained Q evaluations by P and appends zero P towers . It does not approximate-lift the original ciphertext into P. If addFirst=false , its entire first component is zero. KeySwitchDown reduces both accumulated QP components; KeySwitchDownFirstElement reduces only the first. The test checks both addFirst settings and delayed addition of a QP MAC result before reduction. The pinned CKKS EvalFastRotationExt has another ordering requirement: it computes the extended MAC, optionally adds P times c₀ on the Q towers, then applies the automorphism to both QP components . Reduction is deferred. The automorphism map and full rotation API are source-traced here; their exact end-to-end arrays remain P6/P7 work. Do not move the permutation across the selected rotation key without a separate equivalence proof. 7. Full-size fixture and evidence ¶ The deterministic fixture uses FIXEDMANUAL CKKS with multiplicative depth 4, first modulus size 60, scaling modulus size 50, two large digits, and the fixed ring dimension. It produces five Q towers and three P towers . Tower Modulus Primitive root q₀ 1152921504606584833 18043022392882 q₁ 1125899902124033 15995550378 q₂ 1125899911168001 21670117260 q₃ 1125899903827969 938640682 q₄ 1125899908022273 6511788946 p₀ 1152921504598720513 800790938143 p₁ 1152921504597016577 17749908910371 p₂ 1152921504595968001 11469071954203 The configuration requests 50 scaling bits, but q₂ and q₄ are 51-bit primes just above the power-of-two boundary; q₁ and q₃ are 50-bit. All P towers and q₀ are 60-bit. Use the exact table rather than inferring widths from the knob. These exact parameters are asserted in the executable. Pattern generation and diagnostic key generation use fixed integer formulas in that source file. The diagnostic key is not a cryptographic evaluation key . A separate pair of actual generated secret keys supplies a real key-switching key; its fixed arrays are shared by all comparisons in that run. Random key generation is not compared across separate runs. Cases Coverage L=5,4,3,1 × four input patterns Full level, partial last digit, exact digit boundary, partial first digit Zero, all q−1, monomial x¹⁷, deterministic dense residues Zero path, bounds, closed-form coefficient structure, tower-distinct data Actual generated key at L=5 and L=4 Same exact graph with real cryptographic key arrays Intermediate states Digit INTT, complement CRT and NTT, digit assembly, both MACs, P INTT, correction CRT and NTT, final scale Composition and wrappers Fast/full core equality, input immutability, two/three-component update, delayed QP path Negative alternatives Canonical-lift substitution, missing P-key offset, per-digit ModDown Observed on Linux x86_64 with GCC 14.2, Release, NativeInteger 64, and OpenMP off: 18 cases and 117,571,584 residue comparisons passed . All 15 CTests in the OpenFHE-enabled build passed. The deterministic reduced-level fixture found 524,288 residues that distinguish the wrong per-digit reduction order. Every comparison checks all 65536 entries of every involved tower, plus modulus/root order and outer/child format. Intermediate conversion states are observed by calling the same public primitive separately; the tests do not instrument or modify OpenFHE's implementation. Full-core equality checks the composition against the independent formulas. Run the opt-in gate after installing pinned OpenFHE : cmake -S . -B build/openfhe-compat/ntt-build \ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DNTT_ENABLE_OPENFHE_COMPAT=ON \ -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$PWD/build/openfhe-compat/install" cmake --build build/openfhe-compat/ntt-build -j ctest --test-dir build/openfhe-compat/ntt-build \ -R 'openfhe_' --output-on-failure The Hybrid gate links OpenFHE PKE in addition to core. The standalone build still has no OpenFHE dependency. The setup script already builds all modules. 8. Work counts and the next boundary ¶ For one core call, counting transforms per tower rather than per launch: \[ \begin{aligned} \text{Digit INTTs}&=L,\\ \text{Complement NTTs}&=\beta_\ell(L+K)-L,\\ \text{ModDown INTTs}&=2K,\\ \text{ModDown NTTs}&=2L. \end{aligned} \] At M=L=5, K=3, α=3, β=2, this is 11 inverse and 21 forward NTTs . At L=4 it is 10 inverse and 18 forward. These are logical counts from the source graph, not GPU launch counts or measured performance. With 8-byte residues and N=65536, the assembled digits request \(8N\beta_\ell(L+K)\) bytes and the two QP accumulators request \(16N(L+K)\) bytes. Each is 8 MiB at full fixture level. Keys, temporary coefficient buffers, parameters, allocator overhead, and simultaneous lifetime choices are additional. D9 must specify these lifetimes before treating this as a peak-memory bound. D8 freezes this source graph and the exercised array boundary. P1 stays open for D9's device/buffer/stream/cache proposal and D10's architecture decision. P4/P6 must broaden base-conversion and cryptographic fixtures across the production parameter/level/key matrix. This is not a GPU implementation, performance result, or complete CKKS encryption/decryption integration gate. Pinned source references ¶ Hybrid key generation and ordinary/delayed core . title: Run & debug
summary: Run the N=8 example and step through each butterfly in VS Code.
text: Run and debug the NTT in VS Code ¶ Run the N=8 CPU example on macOS, then step through its butterflies in VS Code. CUDA hardware is not required. One-time setup ¶ Open the repository folder in VS Code: code . If VS Code asks, install the recommended extensions: - CMake Tools - C/C++ - LLDB DAP Wait for CMake Tools to finish configuring build/debug . The workspace uses Xcode's lldb-dap ; check that Xcode command-line tools are installed. Run the small example ¶ Open the command palette with Cmd+Shift+P , choose Tasks: Run Task , then choose Run: NTT debug example . The expected output is: natural-order coefficients: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 bit-reversed evaluation values: 5 0 13 8 9 11 5 8 recovered coefficients: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 roundtrip passed Debug it step by step ¶ Open examples/step_by_step.cpp . Click left of the transform.forward(values) line to create a breakpoint. Open Run and Debug with Cmd+Shift+D . Select Debug: NTT example (step by step) . Press F5 . The program first stops at main because stopOnEntry is on. Press F5 again to reach the breakpoint. Press F11 to step into NegacyclicNtt::forward in include/ntt/ntt.hpp . Use F10 to advance one source line at a time. Useful values to add to the Watch panel: stage_pair_distance group_start_index pair_offset upper_index lower_index twiddle_power values For N=8 , the forward transform has three stages with pair distances 4 , 2 , and 1 . title: GPU NTT implementations
summary: Primary-source survey, performance limits, and techniques to evaluate.
text: GPU NTT implementations ¶ Date: 2026-11-05 Project target: CKKS, OpenFHE 1.6.1, Hybrid RNS key switching, NVIDIA RTX 5090 ( sm_120 ), ring dimension 65536 Current repository revision inspected: 363f972 Evidence policy: implementation facts below come only from author papers, official repositories/source code, or NVIDIA documentation. Recommendations and inferences are explicitly labelled. Executive conclusions ¶ Keep exact OpenFHE array compatibility while replacing three bottlenecks: modular division, strided column accesses, and repeated host transfers. Arithmetic: Shoup for fixed twiddles; Barrett/Montgomery for variable products. Layout: compare the baseline with a coalesced transpose/Four-Step path. Thread work: test 4/8 register-held values and fewer block barriers. Integration: keep buffers, keys, and the Hybrid Q → QP → Q pipeline on GPU. Evidence: use FIDESlib as the closest CKKS/OpenFHE comparison; measure complete operations as well as individual NTTs. These are recommendations from the sources below, not measured speedups for this repository. 1. Current implementation ¶ 1.1 Sourced facts from this repository ¶ The CUDA backend uses a negacyclic transform with folded twisting and the following schedule: Forward: DIF column pass followed by a DIF contiguous-tile pass. Inverse: DIT contiguous-tile pass followed by a DIT column pass and a separate scale kernel. Fixed split width and block size of 256. Limb-major storage [limb][coefficient] ; blockIdx.y selects the limb. One full table of powers of psi and psi^-1 , each [limb][N+1] . Two launches per forward transform for N > 256 ; three for inverse. Host upload and download on every public forward , inverse , and pointwise_multiply call; multiply at least keeps its two forward transforms, pointwise product, and inverse together on device. Device multiplication is currently (__uint128_t(a) * b) % q . CPU simulation shares the exact stage bodies with CUDA, and CUDA tests compare exact arrays to a CPU reference and Python big-integer oracle. Primary code: ntt_kernels.cu , dev_core.hpp , mod_arith.hpp , and cuda_ntt.hpp . 1.2 Strengths worth retaining ¶ Recommendation/inference: keep these properties through optimization: The exact mathematical contract: natural-order input, bit-reversed evaluation output, exact inverse, and exact equality to the CPU oracle. The shared simulator/device stage definitions where practical. Optimized arithmetic can sit behind a second policy while the reference policy remains unchanged. Limb-major RNS storage as the baseline. It maps naturally to one modulus per independent transform, pointwise CKKS arithmetic, and OpenFHE's DCRT-tower model. Precomputation at context construction rather than in a hot operation. Named-hardware benchmark provenance and automatic correctness gates. 1.3 Immediate limitations ¶ Observed source behavior Recommended experiment mul_mod uses 128-bit remainder Division-free Shoup and Barrett policies Column threads load a[r + 256*t] : 2,048-byte spacing Coalesced transpose/Four-Step; measure sectors per requested byte Full power table and a barrier after every radix-2 stage Packed twiddles, Shoup quotients, radix-4/8 register work Fixed 256-thread split Tune launch shape for N=65536 and real tower/batch counts Host vectors and synchronous copies Add device views, stream ownership, and reusable scratch Keep the reference path as an oracle. Four logical array movements alone do not establish efficient DRAM access. 2. Libraries and techniques ¶ Reference Technique to evaluate FIDESlib Exact OpenFHE interoperability, device state, transform-boundary fusion GPU-NTT / HEonGPU Merge versus Four-Step schedules, batches, streams, memory pools CKKS-GPU-CORE Eight values per thread and padded shared memory PhantomFHE Radix-8, lazy Shoup ranges, key-switch fusion TensorFHE Operation batching; tensor arithmetic is a separate research path ICICLE Explicit ordering, device domains, and asynchronous APIs cuFHE / cuHE Resident keys and stream-aware operations in a different FHE scheme Theodosian RTX 5090 cache/write-bandwidth limits and fusion tradeoffs Read the implementation evidence and source links 2.1 FIDESlib: the closest match to the project target ¶ FIDESlib describes itself as a server-side CKKS GPU library interoperable with OpenFHE. Its current release states support for OpenFHE 1.6.1, Hybrid key switching, CUDA 12/13, and sm_70 through sm_120 ; it also states that GPU operations are compared bit-for-bit to a patched OpenFHE CPU reference. These are precisely this project's scheme, integration, key-switch, and GPU targets. See the official README and its bit-compatibility design record . Its current 1D NTT uses CT butterflies for forward and GS butterflies for inverse, shared-memory staging, warp-level synchronization below a warp, vectorized 16-byte loads/stores, and Shoup/Barrett arithmetic selected by templates. More importantly, the NTT mode is templated to fuse downstream work including rescale, plaintext multiplication, ModDown, and key-switch dot/accumulate operations. See NTT_1D.cu , INTT_1D.cu , NTTfusions.cuh , and ModMult.cuh . FIDESlib's Hybrid pipeline has dedicated decomposition/ModUp and ModDown kernels, per-device limb partitions, CUDA streams/events, and graph capture in its multi-GPU/scheduling layer. Its high-level RNS object tracks whether a polynomial is in the extended basis and exposes fused key-switch operations. See Conv.cu , LimbPartition.cu , and RNSPoly.cpp . What to absorb: Make exact OpenFHE ciphertext compatibility—not only decrypt-level CKKS tolerance—the integration acceptance target where the same algorithmic formulation is used. Model transform state explicitly: coefficient/evaluation order, normal/extended RNS basis, level, and owning device/stream. Create fusion points at transform boundaries. A generic forward() that always stores a complete intermediate is insufficient for high-performance key switching. Use Shoup constants beside twiddle and key constants. Keep generic Barrett reduction for operands whose multiplier is not precomputed. Test the complete Hybrid formulations. FIDESlib's compatibility record shows that two mathematically valid rotation/key-switch formulations need not produce bit-identical ciphertexts because rounding and noise enter in different orders. Preserve full QP towers during export/import. FIDESlib documents a real compatibility bug caused by truncating extended-basis ciphertexts during materialization. Inference: FIDESlib is both a design reference and a competitor baseline. Before designing a new OpenFHE patch layer, evaluate whether this project's intended contribution is (a) independent kernels integrated directly into stock OpenFHE, (b) an alternative backend with a stable ABI, or (c) improvements that can be contributed to FIDESlib/OpenFHE. Duplicating its entire compatibility layer without a differentiator is high effort. 2.2 GPU-NTT / HEonGPU: Merge NTT and Four-Step NTT ¶ Özcan and Savaş present two GPU algorithms: an iterative “Merge NTT” and a Four-Step NTT. Their target ranges include 2^12..2^16 for HE and larger sizes for proving. They optimize kernel count and block shape for coalesced global access, and report both single-transform latency and concurrent-transform throughput. The paper reports that the iterative form can outperform Four-Step for HE throughput despite Four-Step's locality. See the author paper, Two Algorithms for Fast GPU Implementation of NTT , especially its design and evaluation sections. The current official GPU-NTT repository supports 32- and 64-bit Barrett arithmetic, rejecting moduli above 30 and 61 bits respectively. It specializes ring sizes at compile time, uses per-size kernel configuration tables, supports RNS transforms and batches, accepts CUDA streams, and has different low-ring and multi-stage paths. See the official repository , ntt_launch_impl.cuh , and modular_arith.cuh . HEonGPU uses GPU-NTT inside a GPU-resident BFV/CKKS library. Its paper describes a GPU memory pool, pinned host pool, and multi-stream execution in addition to the NTT itself. See HEonGPU and the official repository . What to absorb: Compare at least two schedules: an improved two-pass/Merge path and a Four-Step or explicit transpose path. Do not assume the current fixed split is optimal. Build a launch table for N=65536 across tower and batch counts; tune it on the 5090. Treat batches as part of the NTT API, not a benchmark wrapper. CKKS naturally supplies many modulus towers and often multiple ciphertext components. Report throughput as well as latency; the best shape changes when enough independent transforms exist to saturate the GPU. Add an allocator and stream contract at the library boundary. 2.3 CKKS-GPU-CORE: memory-centric CKKS and 8-point-per-thread NTT ¶ Jung et al.'s memory-centric CKKS work keeps up to eight NTT values per thread in registers, exchanges through shared memory between local subtransforms, and pads shared memory to reduce bank conflicts. Its basis conversion launches across output limbs and coefficients and accumulates input-limb products before Barrett reduction. See Over 100x Faster Bootstrapping in Fully Homomorphic Encryption through Memory-Centric Optimization with GPUs and the official CKKS-GPU-CORE repository . The source implements two NTT phases, register arrays of eight coefficients per thread, Shoup butterflies, padded shared memory, batched ModUp, and fused ModDown/NTT epilogues. See NttImple.cu and Context.cu . What to absorb: Evaluate radix-8-per-thread as a direct evolution of this repository's two-pass structure: keep eight coefficients in registers, use shared memory only for cross-thread permutations, and reduce full-block barriers. Add padding and profile bank conflicts rather than assuming the [256] shared tile is conflict-free for every access pattern. Co-design basis conversion and NTT buffers. The same extended-basis layout should flow directly into forward NTT and evaluation-key multiplication. Fuse inverse-transform epilogues and forward-transform prologues where the Hybrid formula permits. 2.4 PhantomFHE: radix-8 NWT, lazy Shoup butterflies, and scheme-level fusion ¶ Phantom implements BFV, BGV, and CKKS on CUDA. Its 1D path handles small transforms in one block; its larger 2D path performs radix-8 work with eight register-held values per thread, padded shared-memory exchanges, and two phases. Forward CT butterflies use Shoup multiplication and lazy [0, 2q) / [0, 4q) ranges; inverse GS butterflies defer final reduction/scaling. See the official repository , ntt_1d.cu , fntt_2d.cu , and butterfly.cuh . The Phantom paper describes intra-kernel fusion that reuses register temporaries and inter-kernel fusion across operations such as NWT plus scaling and ModDown plus correction. Its key-switch path connects ModUp, evaluation-key inner product, and ModDown on a supplied stream. See Phantom: A CUDA-Accelerated Word-Wise Homomorphic Encryption Library and eval_key_switch.cu . What to absorb: Use CT forward and GS inverse so compatible orderings can eliminate explicit permutations between NTT, pointwise multiplication, and INTT. Define and prove lazy ranges per butterfly. Reductions are removed only when the next consumer's bound remains safe. Prefer register reuse and boundary fusion over simply increasing shared-memory tile size. Expose the CUDA stream all the way through key switching. 2.5 TensorFHE: tensor-core NTT and operation-level batching ¶ TensorFHE maps a decomposed 32-bit NTT to tensor-core matrix multiplications and emphasizes throughput rather than single-operation latency. It batches CKKS operations and changes layout from (batch, limb, N) to (limb, batch, N) so equal-limb data from different operations is contiguous. It also assigns independent matrix multiplications to separate streams. See the author paper, TensorFHE , especially Sections IV-C and IV-D. What to absorb: Operation-level batching and a layout selectable between [limb][batch][N] and [batch][limb][N] are worth measuring for inference serving. Throughput-oriented inference can benefit from batching several ciphertexts even if one ciphertext already batches all RNS towers. Inference/caution: do not make tensor-core NTT the first implementation path. TensorFHE's arithmetic decomposition and throughput objective differ from OpenFHE's usual 50–60-bit RNS towers and this project's immediate exact-compatibility goal. Establish a fast integer-core Shoup/Barrett backend first; treat tensor cores as a separate experimental backend. 2.6 ICICLE: useful API ideas, not a direct CKKS backend ¶ ICICLE's official NTT API exposes stream, batch size, row/column batch layout, input/output ordering, device-resident flags, async execution, reusable per-device domains, fast-twiddle mode, and an explicit mixed-radix selection. See the official NTT API . What to absorb: Separate an algorithm-independent NTT contract from backend-specific tuning extensions. Make ordering explicit in the type/configuration rather than relying on comments. Initialize and cache a maximum-size domain once, then reuse it for smaller transforms where mathematically compatible. Allow both row-batched and column-batched transforms and device-resident async operation. Inference/caution: ICICLE is primarily a proof-system field library, not an OpenFHE CKKS/Hybrid implementation. Its API concepts transfer; its field choices and transform semantics must not be assumed compatible. Its CUDA backend also has source-availability/licensing conditions that should be checked before any reuse. 2.7 cuFHE/cuHE: historically relevant but not the integration model ¶ cuFHE implements TFHE gates and credits cuHE's GPU NTT; its API supports CUDA streams and keeps a public bootstrapping key initialized on the GPU. See the official cuFHE repository and official cuHE repository . What to absorb: Keep large evaluation/bootstrapping keys resident and permit concurrent independent operations through streams. Inference/caution: TFHE gate bootstrapping has different polynomial sizes, dataflow, and key-switch structure from CKKS Hybrid RNS. cuFHE is not a suitable algorithmic baseline for the OpenFHE integration; it is mainly historical evidence for GPU-resident keys and stream-level concurrency. 2.8 Theodosian: RTX 5090 changes the optimization priority ¶ Theodosian profiles CKKS on RTX 5090 and reports that optimized NTT and basis-conversion kernels are L2-bandwidth-bound. Its NTT uses two kernels; on-the-fly twiddle generation trades arithmetic for fewer twiddle loads. It finds small limb counts underutilize the GPU, uses L2-aware batching until the working set approaches cache capacity, applies multi-polynomial caching and complementary pipelining to Hybrid key-switch stages, and uses CUDA Graphs to reduce launch overhead for static FHE graphs. See Theodosian . The paper reports that batching can hurt after the footprint exceeds the 5090's effective L2 capacity, and that key switching benefits more from cache-aware multi-polynomial execution and graph scheduling than from additional local kernel fusion once the baseline is already heavily fused. What to absorb: Profile L2 read/write throughput and SM-to-L2 traffic on the actual 5090, not only DRAM bandwidth and occupancy. Generate high-volume twiddles on the fly when the arithmetic cost is cheaper than their cache traffic; retain a precomputed mode for low-volume stages. Batch according to measured working-set size. “More batches” is not monotonic. Capture stable key-switch/rotation/inference sequences in CUDA Graphs. Pipeline stages with complementary DRAM/L2 behavior only after dependencies and cache interference are measured. 3. Algorithms and arithmetic ¶ 3.1 CT/GS versus Stockham and Four-Step ¶ Sourced observation: Phantom and FIDESlib use CT forward plus GS inverse; GPU-NTT compares iterative Merge and Four-Step schedules; ICICLE exposes mixed-radix and ordering choices. Recommendation: keep CT/DIF forward and GS/DIT inverse as the first optimized path because the current repository already has the equivalent ordering contract and no bit-reversal pass. Add a Four-Step/transpose prototype only as a benchmarked alternative for the strided column pass. A Stockham autosort path may offer regular accesses and natural ordering, but it normally ping-pongs global buffers; for the target sizes, its extra full-array traffic must beat the cost of the current uncoalesced gather before adoption. 3.2 Mixed radix and register staging ¶ Sourced observation: CKKS-GPU-CORE and Phantom use up to eight values per thread and radix-8 local transforms; GPU-NTT notes higher-radix butterflies as a further optimization. Recommendation: implement radix-4 first, then radix-8: Load 4/8 values per thread using coalesced vectorized transactions. Execute the local stages in registers. Store into padded shared memory for the permutation between local groups. Use warp shuffles where partner lanes remain within a warp. Store once at the end of the phase. This directly reduces table loads, barriers, and shared-memory operations relative to one butterfly per thread per stage. 3.3 Modular multiplication ¶ Sourced observation: GPU-NTT uses Barrett with explicit modulus-bit bounds; Phantom and CKKS-GPU-CORE use Shoup values for twiddles and lazy butterflies; FIDESlib provides Shoup and Barrett paths. Recommendation: use three explicit primitives rather than one universal mul_mod : mul_const_shoup(x, w, w_shoup, q) for twiddles, N^-1 , basis constants, and evaluation-key constants when precomputation is useful. mul_var_barrett(a, b, q, mu) or a benchmarked Montgomery alternative for pointwise variable products. reduce_wide(acc, q, mu) for basis-conversion/key-switch accumulators with a proved accumulator bound. Retain the current __uint128_t % q only as host/device test oracle. Test each optimized primitive exhaustively around 0 , q-1 , lazy bounds, and the maximum supported OpenFHE prime size. 3.4 Twiddle representation ¶ Recommendation/inference: replace [psi^0, ..., psi^N] as the only device representation with: stage/phase-major twiddles in the order consumed by warps; a parallel Shoup quotient table; optional compact “seed” twiddles for on-the-fly expansion in the phase with O(N) table traffic; a metadata record containing transform convention, direction, modulus, ordering, and supported lazy range. The CPU reference can continue to build a simple power table; a packing step should produce the device format and be independently cross-checked. 4. RNS layout and Hybrid state ¶ 4.1 Baseline layout ¶ Recommendation: keep coefficient data limb-major: poly[component][digit-or-batch][limb][coefficient] with coefficient contiguous. This gives coalesced coefficient loads for one limb and makes modulus-specific constants uniform across a block. Provide views/strides so operation-level batching can switch the middle dimensions without copying. 4.2 Extended-basis state ¶ Recommendation: make these states explicit and non-interchangeable: Q, coefficient Q, evaluation QP, coefficient QP, evaluation Each buffer view should carry active Q tower count, P tower count, level, ordering, device, and stream/event ownership. This prevents accidental truncation or redundant transforms at the OpenFHE boundary. 4.3 Target Hybrid pipeline ¶ Recommendation/inference: design the first end-to-end kernel graph around OpenFHE's actual Hybrid formulation, approximately: input c2 in Q/evaluation -> digit partition / inverse NTT as required -> Q-digit to QP basis extension -> forward NTT of extended digits -> evaluation-key multiply-accumulate into two QP outputs -> approximate ModDown QP -> Q -> add/fold c0 as required by the exact OpenFHE operation The exact transform placement and rounding order must be derived from the pinned OpenFHE 1.6.1 source and frozen in compatibility tests. Do not substitute an algebraically equivalent formulation if bit equality is the goal. 4.4 Fusion candidates ¶ High-value, low-ambiguity experiments: INTT final scaling + decomposition pre-scale. Basis-extension output + first forward-NTT load/prologue. Forward-NTT final store + evaluation-key dot product when register and occupancy costs permit. INTT or NTT boundary + ModDown correction. Pointwise accumulation across Hybrid digits, deferring reduction only under a proved bound. Caution: fusion can lower occupancy by increasing registers/shared memory and can prevent cache-friendly scheduling. Theodosian shows additional fusion is not automatically beneficial on RTX 5090. Require profiler evidence for every fused variant. 5. Streams and memory ¶ NVIDIA documents that asynchronous host/device copies require pinned host memory and can overlap with kernels in other streams. It also documents global-to-shared asynchronous copies and pipelines, and states that CUDA Graphs reduce repeated launch setup cost for fixed workflows. See the CUDA Best Practices Guide , asynchronous copy documentation , and CUDA Graphs documentation . Recommended API split: NttContext : immutable moduli, roots, packed twiddles, reduction constants, launch table, and allocator handle. DeviceRnsView : pointer(s), dimensions/strides, basis/domain/order metadata, device, and readiness event. enqueue_forward/inverse(view, stream) : no allocation, no synchronization, no host copy. convenience host methods: pinned staging plus explicit or documented synchronization. reusable scratch arena sized for maximum supported level/digit count. captured CUDA graphs for fixed ring dimension, level, digit count, and operation sequence. Recommendation/inference: try cuda::memcpy_async /pipeline only after the coalesced phase layout is fixed. The current column gather has no useful sequential “next tile” per block to hide without first changing data ownership; async copy cannot repair uncoalesced addresses. 6. Correctness and measurement ¶ 6.1 Correctness ladder ¶ Arithmetic primitive versus __uint128_t % q , including adversarial bounds and every OpenFHE modulus. Butterfly and single-stage exact tests for CT/DIF and GS/DIT, including lazy-range invariants. Complete forward/inverse exact equality against the existing CPU and Python oracle for every N in {65536} . RNS batches across realistic CKKS tower counts, not only three limbs. Negacyclic polynomial multiplication exact equality. Basis conversion exact equality to the pinned OpenFHE 1.6.1 implementation. Hybrid relinearization and rotation: exact ciphertext comparison where formulation and code generation permit; decrypt-error comparison as a secondary semantic test. Long operation sequences and inference circuits, including level/scale/noise metadata and repeated rotations. 6.2 Required performance views ¶ For each ring dimension, modulus bit-width, and tower count: kernel-only forward and inverse latency using CUDA events; end-to-end latency with pinned and pageable host transfer reported separately; transforms/second for batches of towers, ciphertext components, and independent ciphertexts; full polynomial multiply latency; Hybrid key switch, relinearization, and rotation latency; complete inference latency and peak device memory; bytes read/written, achieved DRAM bandwidth, L2 read/write throughput, global load/store efficiency, bank conflicts, register count, occupancy, and launch count from Nsight Compute/Systems; cold setup, warm steady state, and CUDA Graph replay as distinct measurements. 6.3 Baselines ¶ This repository's current pre-Barrett kernel, labelled clearly as a correctness baseline. Optimized kernel with identical transfers. GPU-NTT or another standalone GPU NTT with matched modulus/order/batch where license and semantics permit. FIDESlib 2.2/OpenFHE 1.6.1 for NTT microbenchmarks and, more importantly, full Hybrid key switch/rotation. Stock OpenFHE 1.6.1 CPU, with build flags and thread count recorded. Do not compare one implementation's kernel-only time with another's transfer-inclusive time, nor one-limb latency with an entire RNS polynomial. 7. Priorities ¶ Priority Deliverable P0 Real-GPU exact checks, arithmetic policies, device-buffer/stream contract P1 Shoup/Barrett kernels, register staging, coalesced layout, measured dispatch P2 Explicit Q/QP state, exact basis conversion, resident keys, safe fusion P3 Hoisting, operation batching, graph replay, whole-inference profiling The integration plan tracks completion; the benchmark plan defines the workload and acceptance record. The priorities here do not mark a roadmap gate complete. 8. Licensing and provenance ¶ This section is informational, not legal advice. FIDESlib: MIT license in its official repository. Its OpenFHE interoperability currently depends on patches, which should be reviewed separately for upstream/license provenance. GPU-NTT: Apache-2.0. HEonGPU: check the repository's current license before copying code; concepts described by the paper can be independently implemented. PhantomFHE: GPLv3. Copying its source into a differently licensed project can impose copyleft obligations. Use the paper and behavior as design evidence unless the project intentionally adopts compatible licensing. CKKS-GPU-CORE: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 in the repository. The non-commercial/share-alike terms make direct code reuse unsuitable for many projects. Independently implement paper-level ideas and preserve clean-room provenance. ICICLE CUDA backend: source availability and the backend license have changed across releases. Verify the exact version's terms before any reuse. cuFHE/cuHE: their official repositories state their licenses; verify individual files before reuse. Recommendation: continue the repository's clean-room policy. Cite papers and inspect behavior/interfaces, but write original kernels. If code is adapted from MIT/Apache sources, preserve required notices and record the exact file/commit. Do not copy GPL or CC BY-NC-SA kernel code unless the project's license decision explicitly permits it. 9. Next implementation steps ¶ The survey supports the following immediate implementation sequence: Introduce arithmetic policies and implement ShoupTwiddle plus BarrettVariable , with exact tests. Add a device-buffer/stream API without removing the current host-vector facade. Instrument and benchmark the existing two-pass kernel on RTX 5090 using CUDA events and Nsight. Implement one radix-8, padded-shared-memory variant and one coalesced transpose/Four-Step variant. Select per-size/per-batch winners through a dispatch table. Build the Q/QP state/layout and OpenFHE 1.6.1 compatibility harness before implementing base conversion. Optimize and report the full Hybrid key-switch graph, with FIDESlib as the central GPU baseline. Benchmarking and autotuning across GPU parameters and implementation variants are a permanent project workstream, not a one-time comparison. The concrete matrix, required counters, reproducibility record, dispatch rules, and acceptance gates are defined in benchmark-tuning-plan.md . The HTML explainer should then be updated to show both the current correctness schedule and the selected production schedule. It should no longer imply that low nominal global byte count alone means efficient VRAM access; it should visualize coalescing, register-held radix-8 work, padded shared memory, and the complete Q -> QP -> Q Hybrid dataflow. Primary sources ¶ Papers, repositories, and NVIDIA documentation Özcan and Savaş, Two Algorithms for Fast GPU Implementation of NTT ; GPU-NTT source . Özcan and Savaş, HEonGPU ; HEonGPU source . Yang et al., Phantom ; PhantomFHE source . Jung et al., Over 100x Faster Bootstrapping through Memory-Centric Optimization with GPUs ; CKKS-GPU-CORE source . Fan et al., TensorFHE . Agulló-Domingo et al., FIDESlib source and documentation . Choi et al., Theodosian . Ingonyama, ICICLE NTT API . Vernam Lab, cuFHE and cuHE . NVIDIA, CUDA C++ Programming Guide , CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide , and Nsight Compute documentation .

title: Choosing the GPU
summary: Compare hardware for exact u32/u64 modular arithmetic and CKKS workloads.
text: Choosing a GPU for CKKS ¶ Hardware assessment recorded on 2026-11-06. The RTX 5090 choice is provisional; production selection requires the benchmark gate below. Specifications and historical prices are reference values, not current quotes or kernel timings. Decision ¶ Role GPU Reason Primary development RTX 5090 32 GB, 1.792 TB/s bandwidth, Blackwell sm_120 Compatibility control RTX 4090 Ada sm_89 ; useful when owned or rented More capacity / enterprise support RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB ECC; evaluate when the working set exceeds 32 GB Later production comparison H200 / B200 Larger HBM and bandwidth; benchmark the complete workload Use the 5090 for development. Select a production GPU only after measuring resident memory and end-to-end Hybrid key switching. Why FP8 and FP16 marketing does not answer our question ¶ These kernels perform exact modular u32 / u64 arithmetic and move RNS data. Tensor TOPS do not measure that workload. NVIDIA's Tensor Core type table does not list arbitrary u32 / u64 modular operations. Relevant primitives include mul.hi , mul.lo , and mul.wide and __umul64hi . The native instruction table does not publish a directly comparable 64-bit multiply throughput. Measure Shoup/Barrett instruction chains rather than deriving an “INT64 TOPS” ranking. Official specification comparison ¶ Bandwidth is a peak specification. INT32 is published non-Tensor throughput, not modular multiplication performance. “—” means no comparable value was published in the cited product material.
