RTX 5090 memory correction is not the same enterprise reliability/support offering as RTX PRO or data-center ECC. L40S L2 is not stated on its product page; the full AD102/L40 figure must not be silently substituted. Primary sources for the table ¶ Open NVIDIA specification sources and qualifications NVIDIA's CUDA GPU compute-capability list maps RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell to CC 12.0, B200 to CC 10.0, H100/H200 to CC 9.0, RTX 4090/L40S to CC 8.9, and A100 to CC 8.0. NVIDIA's CUDA architecture/toolkit matrix lists first toolkit support and ongoing support; CUDA 12.8 added sm_100 , sm_101 , and sm_120 compiler support. The RTX Blackwell architecture whitepaper provides the RTX 5090's 170 SMs, 21,760 CUDA cores, 32 GB GDDR7, 1.792 TB/s, 96 MB L2, 575 W, 104.8 INT32 TOPS, and built-in GDDR7 single-bit correction. It also provides RTX 4090 comparison figures. The RTX PRO Blackwell architecture whitepaper provides 96 GB ECC GDDR7, 1.792 TB/s, 128 MB L2, 600 W, and 126 INT32 TOPS. The shorter product datasheet confirms the main board specifications. The official L40S product page specifies 48 GB GDDR6 with ECC, 864 GB/s, 18,176 CUDA cores, and 350 W. The Ada architecture whitepaper documents the 96 MB L2 full-AD102/L40 configuration; the current L40S page does not separately state L2. The A100 product page specifies 80 GB HBM2e, 2,039 GB/s for SXM, and 400 W. NVIDIA's Ampere architecture analysis documents 40 MB L2 and SECDED protection of HBM, L2, L1, and register files. The H100 datasheet specifies 80 GB, 3.35 TB/s, and up to 700 W. NVIDIA's Hopper architecture analysis documents 50 MB L2 and its architecture comparison. The H200 datasheet specifies 141 GB HBM3e, 4.8 TB/s, and up to 700 W. NVIDIA's HGX component table specifies H100/H200/B200 capacity and bandwidth and a configurable limit up to 1 kW per GPU. The Blackwell tuning guide documents B200/GB200's 180 GB memory support and 126 MB L2. NVIDIA's GPU memory-error management guide documents HBM ECC correction and error-management behavior for Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell data-center families. Cost and availability snapshot ¶ Prices in the original assessment were regional, time-sensitive reference points. Compare the complete workstation or VM cost and measured work per hour. Read the historical pricing evidence Prices are volatile, regional, and not directly comparable between a bare card and a complete cloud VM. The following are official reference points, not a purchasing quote: NVIDIA lists the RTX 5090 from $1,999 . NVIDIA launched the RTX 4090 from $1,599 , but its current official product page no longer provides a meaningful live purchase price. A used or already-owned 4090 can still be economical; a new project should not assume launch-price availability. NVIDIA Marketplace listed a partner RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition at $14,079.99 when this report was checked. That is about seven times the RTX 5090 list price for three times the VRAM, professional ECC positioning, MIG, enterprise support, and about 20% more published non-Tensor INT32 peak—not seven times the kernel performance. See the official NVIDIA Marketplace listing . Google Cloud lists an RTX PRO 6000 96 GB virtual-workstation GPU at $1.09565 per GPU-hour in the first displayed region, before the VM, storage, network, and any licensing charges. The page states that price and availability vary by region. See Google Cloud GPU pricing . AWS Capacity Blocks list examples of about $5.97 per H100-hour and $14.21–$14.80 per B200-hour , sold as eight-GPU blocks in the shown regions. These are suitable for bounded cross-GPU experiments, not evidence that either card is cost-effective for daily development. See AWS Capacity Blocks pricing . Inference: local RTX 5090 ownership is the best development economics when the card remains well utilized. A cloud RTX PRO 6000 is an attractive way to validate the 96 GB path without buying a workstation card. H200/B200 rentals should be delayed until optimized kernels and a fixed benchmark harness exist, otherwise expensive time will mostly measure unfinished code. Interpretation for this project ¶ Comparison Published difference What still needs measurement 5090 versus 4090 1.78× bandwidth, 33% more VRAM/L2, about 2.54× INT32 peak Actual NTT and key-switch speedup PRO 6000 versus 5090 Same bandwidth, 3× VRAM, 33% more L2, about 20% more INT32 peak Benefit from capacity, reliability, and batching H200/B200 versus RTX Larger HBM and higher bandwidth Modular arithmetic, cache behavior, and end-to-end cost At N=65536, a 40-tower polynomial uses 65536 × 40 × 8 = 20 MiB . Evaluation keys, QP temporaries, twiddles, and concurrent ciphertexts can consume much more. Record peak memory with all keys resident before choosing capacity. Recommended acquisition strategy ¶ Develop and tune on RTX 5090; check workstation power and cooling. Retain or rent RTX 4090 for cross-architecture correctness and timing. Evaluate RTX PRO 6000 if measured residency exceeds 28 GB or enterprise reliability/support is required. Rent H200/B200 after the optimized kernels and fixed harness exist. Mandatory cross-GPU benchmark gate ¶ Run the same commit, parameters, and timing boundaries. Record toolkit, clocks, power policy, median, p95, and peak memory. Layer Required cases Arithmetic u32/u64 add/subtract, high/low products, Shoup, Barrett, reference remainder; registers and spills Memory / NTT Coalesced copy, strided gather, L2/DRAM cases, forward/inverse at N=65536, realistic tower counts Hybrid ModUp, ModDown, decomposition, key MAC, relinearization, rotation; one request and batches Correctness Exact pinned-OpenFHE arrays at every intermediate boundary See the benchmark plan for counters and result records. Keep kernel-only and transfer-inclusive timing separate. Selection rule ¶ Keep RTX 5090 as primary if the complete resident set fits and its end-to-end latency is within 15% of the fastest tested card. If only capacity blocks it, compare RTX PRO 6000 with H200 rental and deployment costs. Use profiling to separate memory-layout limits from modular-multiply limits before redesigning arithmetic or selecting hardware. Bottom line ¶ RTX 5090 is the development choice. Production hardware remains an open, measured decision; FP8/FP16 Tensor figures do not settle it.

title: Benchmarks & tuning
summary: Workload matrix, profiling evidence, and per-device kernel selection.
text: GPU NTT benchmark and tuning plan ¶ Primary target: NVIDIA RTX 5090 ( sm_120 ) Cross-architecture control: NVIDIA RTX 4090 ( sm_89 ) Workload target: OpenFHE 1.6.1 CKKS with Hybrid key switching Ring dimensions: 65536 Choose kernels using exact checks and measured latency or throughput at N=65536. Record the GPU, CKKS parameters, batch shape, and transfer boundary. 1. Implementations to compare ¶ Each implementation must preserve the same transform convention and pass the same exact correctness gates. Current radix-2 two-pass implementation using reference modular arithmetic. Two-pass implementation with Shoup twiddle multiplication and Barrett or Montgomery variable multiplication. Radix-4 register-staged implementation. Radix-8 register-staged implementation with padded shared memory. Coalesced Four-Step/transpose implementation. Fused variants used by base conversion and Hybrid key switching. Compare GPU-NTT and FIDESlib only when transform semantics, modulus limits, RNS workload, and timing boundaries match. 2. Workload matrix ¶ The minimum matrix is: Axis Values Ring dimension 2^16 Modulus width OpenFHE-compatible 50, 55, 59/60-bit primes Active RNS towers representative shallow, medium, and deep CKKS levels Polynomial count one component, full ciphertext, key-switch digits Batch size 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , then L2-capacity-limited sweep Direction forward, inverse, forward–pointwise–inverse Objective single-operation latency and steady-state throughput Transfer policy device-resident, pinned end-to-end, pageable end-to-end GPU RTX 5090 primary; RTX 4090 control Take tower and Hybrid digit counts from the pinned OpenFHE parameter sets. Three-limb synthetic fixtures alone are insufficient. 3. GPU and kernel parameters to tune ¶ Tune or record all of the following: threads per block and blocks per transform; values and butterflies per thread; radix and number of stages fused per kernel; tile/split dimensions and transpose shape; register count per thread and register spilling; static/dynamic shared memory per block and bank conflicts; active blocks and warps per SM; warp-shuffle versus shared-memory exchange boundaries; twiddle layout, Shoup table layout, and on-the-fly twiddle generation; lazy-reduction range and reduction frequency; RNS limb, ciphertext, and operation batch layout; CUDA stream count, asynchronous copies, and CUDA Graph replay; scratch-buffer reuse and allocator behavior. Retain ptxas -v reports and Nsight occupancy. Select by end-to-end performance, not register count alone. 4. Measurements ¶ Timing ¶ CUDA-event kernel-only latency for every kernel and complete transform; transfer-inclusive latency, separating pinned and pageable host memory; transforms per second and coefficients/towers processed per second; full polynomial multiplication latency; Hybrid key switch, relinearization, rotation, and hoisted-rotation latency; complete encrypted-inference latency and peak device memory; cold setup, warm steady state, and CUDA Graph replay separately. Report median, p5, and p95 after warm-up. Store raw samples so later summaries can be regenerated without rerunning the GPU. Hardware counters ¶ achieved DRAM and L2 bandwidth; global load/store transaction efficiency; L2 hit rate and read/write sectors; shared-memory bank conflicts; registers per thread, spills, occupancy, and eligible warps; SM and memory-pipeline utilization; kernel-launch count and synchronization gaps. The current column pass must specifically record memory sectors per requested byte because its neighboring-thread coefficient addresses are 2,048 bytes apart. 5. Reproducibility record ¶ Every result row must include: GPU name, compute capability, clocks, power mode, and memory size; driver, CUDA toolkit/runtime, compiler, CMake flags, and git commit; implementation/variant ID and all tuned launch parameters; N , modulus bits, actual moduli or parameter-set ID, tower count, digit count, batch shape, transform ordering, and transfer policy; correctness-gate result and profiler command/version; whether setup, allocation, transfers, and synchronization are included. Results without this header are exploratory and must not appear in published comparison tables. 6. Tuning procedure ¶ Run exact arithmetic and transform gates for the candidate variant. Reject variants that spill unexpectedly, exceed resource limits, or violate lazy-reduction bounds. Sweep launch and staging parameters at N=65536. Profile the best latency and throughput candidates with Nsight Compute. Repeat using realistic RNS tower and Hybrid digit batches. Validate finalists on RTX 4090 to identify architecture-specific choices. Record the winner in a dispatch table keyed by GPU capability, ring dimension, tower/batch range, and latency/throughput mode. Re-run the complete Hybrid key-switch and inference benchmarks. A locally faster NTT variant is accepted only if it improves the target pipeline or supplies a clearly justified fallback. 7. Acceptance gates ¶ Exact forward/inverse agreement for every supported N and OpenFHE modulus. No silent fallback to device-side integer remainder in optimized kernels. No benchmark mixes kernel-only and end-to-end timing boundaries. A selected latency and throughput implementation exists for N=65536 on RTX 5090. RTX 4090 results either validate the same dispatch or document a separate one. Full Hybrid key-switch and inference results accompany NTT microbenchmarks. The HTML explainer identifies which schedule is the correctness baseline and which implementation the tuner selected for each workload class.

title: Writing & publishing
summary: Preview the site, add a daily journal entry, and publish the HTML documentation.
text: Writing and publishing the project notebook ¶ Edit Markdown and the three interactive HTML lessons in docs/ . Build the site locally, then export it to the personal website. Generated HTML is not source. Preview locally ¶ python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r docs/requirements.txt .venv/bin/python scripts/build_docs.py --check python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory build/docs-site Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ . Rebuild and refresh after editing. The interactive source HTML also works independently. Read the site ¶ The left sidebar switches pages. On this page lists the current page's sections and highlights your reading position. On smaller screens, use Menu for pages and Sections for headings. Search opens from the top bar or Ctrl+K / Cmd+K . Learn pages explain the mathematics and code; Research records evidence; Plans track gates; the Daily journal records dated results. Calendar dates and roadmap working days are separate: publishing a note does not complete a gate. Add a daily entry ¶ python3 scripts/new_journal.py --date 2026-11-10 --title "Describe the outcome" The helper creates a draft without overwriting an existing entry. Append to an existing day. Keep the title , date , summary , phase , and status metadata. Fill all six required sections: Section Record Outcome What changed Reasoning Evidence behind the decision Changes Links to code and documents Verification Observed checks, hardware, and limits Open questions What remains unresolved Next step The next deliverable Use status: published when complete; drafts stay off the site. Label reconstructed history and cite commits. Update the integration plan when a gate changes. Its tracker supplies the homepage checkpoint. Add or edit an article ¶ Register new documents in docs/site.json with source, URL, title, group, and summary. Use relative links to documents and code; the builder converts them to HTML routes or revision-pinned GitHub links. Use ## headings for main sections and ### for subsections. Main headings populate the section sidebar automatically, including headings in HTML lessons. Existing anchors are preserved. Tables scroll inside the article. Write inline math as \(...\) and display math as \[...\] . KaTeX is bundled locally. Put long reference material in <details markdown="1"> with a clear <summary> ; keep the main conclusion visible. Search includes collapsed text. Validate before publishing ¶ .venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests/docs -v .venv/bin/python scripts/build_docs.py --check node --test tests/docs/*.test.cjs The build validates catalog coverage, journal metadata, and local links, assets, and heading fragments. The site supports project subpaths. The Node checks run the pages' actual inline scripts. The work-distribution checks cover N=65536 in both directions, stage controls, boundary selections, and complete per-stage index coverage. The handwritten-derivation checks compare DIT and negacyclic DIF butterfly results with independent direct NTT sums and check full-size twiddle/index boundaries. Node.js 22+ is required; no packages are needed. These checks do not replace browser inspection or CUDA execution. The separate C++ column proof executes the production stage helper on CPU: cmake -S . -B build cmake --build build --target ntt_column_mapping_tests ntt_device_sim ctest --test-dir build -R 'column_mapping_check|inverse_column_check|device_schedule_check' --output-on-failure The column check executes the real shared stage helper with tagged power tables at N=65536. It probes the input pair, ladder multiplier, and twiddle selection for every column butterfly. This is CPU verification, not a native CUDA build or a GPU race check. The inverse gate additionally checks reciprocal-table selection, the factor of two from one forward/inverse stage pair, and full N-inverse normalization with valid roots for two primes at N=65536. For D4, run: cmake --build build --target ntt_tile_mapping_tests ctest --test-dir build -R tile_mapping_check --output-on-failure It probes every row butterfly at N=65536 in both directions and checks the two-pass stage lists and global endpoint coverage at N=65536 and small-size boundaries. Run a full build and ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure to include the D3 and D4 gates together. The Python documentation suite also includes D5 source-contract checks for the allocation/copy/API map. These inspect C++ source text and pin byte-count arithmetic; they do not compile CUDA, inject failures, or validate runtime resource cleanup. See CUDA buffers and dataflow . The D6 arithmetic contract has two CPU gates: cmake --build build --target ntt_arithmetic_contract_tests ctest --test-dir build -R 'arithmetic_' --output-on-failure They check compiled primitives against Python big integers and run full-size 50/55/60-bit transform patterns. They are not native CUDA tests. OpenFHE representation gate ¶ The optional OpenFHE build registers both openfhe_exact_compat and openfhe_representation_contract . The D7 contract explains the pinned source, exact array convention, and test command. These are CPU tests against OpenFHE 1.6.1; GPU execution remains a separate gate. Publish with GitHub Pages ¶ Add the notebook to the personal website ¶ From this repository: .venv/bin/python scripts/export_website.py --website-root /path/to/minnow54426.github.io Review, commit, and push the generated systems/ntt-gpu/ files in the website repository. Its Pages workflow publishes the site. Open the notebook . The exporter refreshes managed files only and adds a return link to the personal website. Navigation, search, and math also work in local previews. Standalone project Pages deployment ¶ Ordinary pushes to ntt-gpu build a preview artifact; they do not publish the personal website. For an optional standalone site, set repository Settings → Pages → Source → GitHub Actions , then manually run the Documentation workflow with deploy_standalone enabled. Its URL is minnow54426.github.io/ntt-gpu .
